items.title: Introduction
items.text:
Flaskteroids is a Python MVC framework built on Flask, SQLAlchemy, and Celery. It brings models, routes, templates, forms, background jobs, and email into a shared application workflow.

These guides teach you how to build with Flaskteroids. Start with the tutorial if you are new, or choose a component guide for the feature you are working on.

items.title: Build your first application
items.text:
Getting started walks you through a product catalog. You will create a model, display products, and build forms to add, edit, and delete them. You need basic Python and HTML knowledge, but no experience with the underlying libraries.

The rest of the store tutorial adds one feature at a time:

  1. Login and product images — protect catalog changes and upload a photo.
  2. Restock notifications — connect subscriptions, inventory changes, background jobs, and email.
  3. Test the store — check the workflows you have built.
  4. Prepare for deployment — review security and try the generated Docker setup.

Each part continues in the same application. You can stop after the first part with a working catalog.

items.title: Find a guide
items.text: Component guides explain a feature through focused examples. They assume you have a generated application, but do not require completing the store tutorial.

items.title: Models
items.text:
• Model basics — create, query, validate, and save records.
  • Associations — connect models and work with related records.
  • Callbacks — run shared behavior during a record's lifecycle.
  • Fields — choose column types and understand submitted values.
  • Attribute encryption — protect sensitive model data.

items.title: Routing and controllers
items.text:
• Routing — connect URLs to actions.
  • Controller basics — handle input and choose a response.
  • Rate limits — limit repeated requests.
  • Building an API — build and test a JSON API.

items.title: Views and frontend
items.text:
• Templates and helpers — render pages and share presentation logic.
  • Forms — accept input and help users correct mistakes.
  • Turbo Frames and Streams — add inline navigation and page updates.
  • Assets — add styles and images, then build production files.
  • JavaScript with import maps — load modules without a build step.

items.title: Background work and email
items.text:
• Background jobs — move work outside a request.
  • Mailers — compose, preview, test, and deliver email.

items.title: Files and rich text
items.text:
• Attachments — upload files and control download access.
  • Rich text — edit and display formatted content safely.

items.title: Application setup and testing
items.text:
• Project structure — find where code and configuration belong.
  • Configuration — choose settings and manage secrets.
  • Using the command line — generate components and run application tasks.
  • Middleware — wrap requests before controller dispatch.
  • Internationalization — translate text and localize dates.
  • Testing — test models, requests, jobs, mail, and browser workflows.

Unless a guide says otherwise, run commands from your application root with bin/flask. You do not need to activate the virtual environment.

To help improve these pages, see Writing guides.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Start with the generated defaults and change settings as your application needs them. Run the commands in this guide from your application directory.

What you want to configure Where to put it Settings shared by every environment config/application.py Development, test, or production overrides config/environments/ Database connections config/database.yml API keys and other secrets Encrypted credentials External library setup config/initializers/

Environment settings are applied after application-wide settings, so they can override the shared defaults.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Choose where application and environment settings belong.
  • Configure a database and keep secrets in encrypted credentials.
  • Prepare configuration for scripts and deployment.

items.title: Application settings
items.text:
Start with config/application.py for settings shared by every environment:

from flaskteroids.application import Application as FlaskteroidsApplication
from config.boot import ROOT


class Application(FlaskteroidsApplication):
    root = ROOT

    def configure(self, config):
        config.load_defaults("0.1")
        config.x.payments.provider = "stripe"

config.load_defaults() selects the framework defaults for a version. Updating Flaskteroids does not change this choice automatically. To adopt newer defaults, change the version passed to load_defaults().

The application generator selects browser defaults unless you pass --api, which sets config.api_only = True. See Building an API for API application setup and controller behavior.

items.title: Environments
items.text:
Flaskteroids selects the environment in this order:

  1. The explicit environment= argument to Application.initialize().
  2. FLASKTEROIDS_ENV.
  3. development.

FLASKTEROIDS_ENV selects Flaskteroids configuration, not Flask's debugger. Use bin/flask run --debug to enable the debugger.

Framework-provided environment variables use the FLASKTEROIDS_ prefix, including FLASKTEROIDS_DATABASE_URL, FLASKTEROIDS_SECRET_KEY_BASE, FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY, FLASKTEROIDS_ATTACHMENTS_SERVICE, and FLASKTEROIDS_ENCRYPTION_*. The prefix applies only to environment variables: Python settings such as config.secret_key_base and config.encryption.primary_key, and credential names such as secret_key_base and encryption, remain unprefixed. Dependency-owned variables such as Flask's FLASK_APP and Celery's CELERY_BROKER_URL retain their native names.

Put environment-specific overrides in the matching file. For example:

# config/environments/production.py
import os


def configure(config):
    config.eager_load = True
    config.consider_all_requests_local = False
    config.require_master_key = True
    config.mailer.perform_deliveries = True
    config.jobs.broker_url = os.environ.get(
        "CELERY_BROKER_URL", config.jobs.broker_url
    )

The current environment is available from the application:

application.env.name
application.env.development
application.env.test
application.env.production

Read other environment variables with os.environ in your configuration.

items.title: Database configuration
items.text:
Define database connections in config/database.yml:

default: &default
  adapter: sqlite3
  pool: 5

development:
  <<: *default
  database: storage/development.sqlite3

test:
  <<: *default
  database: storage/test.sqlite3

production:
  url: ${FLASKTEROIDS_DATABASE_URL}

The generated app uses SQLite for development and tests. For another database, install its driver and set FLASKTEROIDS_DATABASE_URL:

For PostgreSQL:

uv add 'psycopg[binary]'
export FLASKTEROIDS_DATABASE_URL='postgresql+psycopg://app:password@localhost/my_app'

Or for MySQL:

uv add 'PyMySQL[rsa]'
export FLASKTEROIDS_DATABASE_URL='mysql+pymysql://app:password@localhost/my_app'

Use ${NAME} in YAML to read an environment variable, or ${NAME:-default} to supply a fallback. Connection settings are chosen in this order:

  1. An explicit url in database.yml.
  2. FLASKTEROIDS_DATABASE_URL.
  3. Individual settings such as adapter, database, username, and password.

items.title: Encrypted credentials
items.text:
Credentials let you keep API keys and other secrets in an encrypted YAML file. The shared file is config/credentials.yml.enc; its local key is config/master.key. Encryption uses AES-256-GCM.

Commit the encrypted file, never the key. Generated Git and container ignore files already exclude the key. In production, supply it through FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY rather than putting it in your image.

Open the editor to add secrets:

bin/flask credentials:edit

For example, add this YAML in the editor:

payments:
  api_key: your-secret-key

To inspect decrypted values, run bin/flask credentials:show. Its output is plaintext: do not copy it into logs or issue reports.

items.title: Separate credentials for each environment
items.text:
Use --environment to edit or inspect an environment-specific file:

bin/flask credentials:edit --environment production
bin/flask credentials:show --environment production

The edit command creates these files if needed:

config/credentials/production.yml.enc
config/credentials/production.key

Environment-specific credentials replace, rather than merge with, shared credentials. Include every secret that environment needs. The key is read from FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY first, then the corresponding key file.

items.title: Read credentials in Python
items.text:
Credentials are available through the application:

application.credentials.secret_key_base
application.credentials.payments.api_key
application.credentials["payments"]["api_key"]

In production, set config.require_master_key = True so startup fails if credentials cannot be decrypted.

The keys have different purposes:

Key Purpose Credentials master key Decrypt the credentials file secret_key_base Sign sessions, CSRF tokens, and password-reset tokens encryption.primary_key / encryption.deterministic_key Encrypt model attributes and rich-text bodies

Do not reuse the master or signing key for model data. See Attribute encryption to set up encrypted attributes.

items.title: Initializers
items.text:
Use initializers for setup that should run once during application startup, such as creating an external service client:

# config/initializers/payments.py
from flaskteroids import application
from payments import Client

application.extensions["payments"] = Client(
    api_key=application.credentials.payments.api_key
)

Keep database queries out of initializers when possible. Query from an action, job, or function when the data is needed, so database setup can run before tables exist.

items.title: Request limits
items.text:
Set request limits in configure, rather than in request or controller callbacks:

config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"] = 16 * 1024 * 1024  # Total request body: 16 MiB
config["MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE"] = 500_000         # Each multipart text field
config["MAX_FORM_PARTS"] = 1_000                # Multipart fields and files

Requests that exceed these limits are rejected with 413 Content Too Large.

items.title: Using models and jobs in scripts
items.text:
Requests and jobs run inside an application context. In scripts, open one before using models or enqueueing jobs:

from app.jobs.my_job import MyJob
from app.models.user import User
from config.environment import application

with application.app_context():
    user = User.find(1)
    MyJob().perform_later(user_id=user.id)

An application context provides configuration and a database session; it is not a transaction. A standalone model save commits before returning. To group writes, use with Model.transaction():; an exception escaping the block rolls them back.

When the context ends, it closes the session and rolls back unfinished work. It does not undo earlier standalone commits. Native SQLAlchemy writes require an explicit commit or transaction. See Models.

items.title: Component settings
items.text:
Configure a component when you add it to your application. Its guide explains the settings alongside the workflow they affect:

  • Middleware — wrap requests and change the stack.
  • View helpers — choose helpers included in controller views.
  • Internationalization — enable locales and load translation catalogs.
  • Background jobs — select a broker and queue adapter.
  • Mail delivery — configure a sender and SMTP.
  • Attachment storage — select a file storage service.

items.title: Preparing for deployment
items.text:
On a fresh checkout, run bin/setup to install dependencies and prepare the database. Before deploying database changes, prepare your production environment:

FLASKTEROIDS_ENV=production bin/flask db:prepare

Start PostgreSQL or MySQL yourself and give the application permission to create its database. If your host provisions it for you, use db:migrate to apply changes. PostgreSQL preparation also needs access to the postgres database; choose another with config.database_tasks.maintenance_database if your host requires it. See database commands for the everyday workflow.

Provide FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY when starting production so the app can read its encrypted credentials. Keep the key out of your image and source control. SQLite databases and local uploads need persistent storage.

The generated Docker setup prepares the database before starting the web app. When deploying several instances, arrange one release step for migrations instead of letting every instance run them. Your generated deploy/README.md walks through that setup.

items.title: Getting started with Flaskteroids
items.text:
Welcome! In this guide, you will build a small product catalog called store. You will create products, display them in a browser, and build forms to add, edit, and delete them.

After working through this guide, you will know how to:

  • Create and run a Flaskteroids application.
  • Define a model, migrate its table, and validate input.
  • Follow a request through routes, controllers, and views.
  • Build a create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) interface.

You need basic Python and HTML knowledge, but no experience with Flask, SQLAlchemy, or Celery.

items.title: About the store tutorial
items.text:
This guide is the first part of a tutorial. You can stop with a working catalog, or continue to build a fuller store, one feature at a time:

  1. Getting started — build the product catalog on this page.
  2. Add login and product images.
  3. Add restock notifications.
  4. Test the store.
  5. Prepare the store for deployment.

Each part continues in the same application. The component guides explain individual features when you want to explore them without following the whole tutorial.

items.title: The Flaskteroids approach
items.text:
Flaskteroids is a Python MVC framework built with Flask, SQLAlchemy, and Celery. It gives these components a shared application structure and workflow. Two ideas guide that workflow:

  • Convention over configuration: names and directories tell the framework where your models, controllers, templates, and jobs belong.
  • Don't repeat yourself: migrations describe database structure; models describe behavior; reusable templates and callbacks keep shared logic together.

You can use the underlying libraries when needed, but ordinary application work should not require managing ORM mappings or database sessions yourself.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Install these tools before continuing:

  • Python 3.14 or newer.
  • Git and Bash.
  • uv.
  • A code editor.

The shell commands in this guide assume a POSIX environment, such as Linux, macOS, or Windows through WSL. SQLite is included with Python; you do not need a separate database server for this tutorial.

Start by creating and activating a virtual environment, then install Flaskteroids:

python3 -m venv flaskteroids-env
source flaskteroids-env/bin/activate
pip install flaskteroids

Generate your application in a new directory:

flask new store
cd store

The generator creates the project, installs its dependencies with uv into its own .venv, and prepares the development database. It also creates encrypted credentials and a local master key.

From now on, run commands inside store, using bin/flask. This wrapper uses the application's virtual environment automatically, so you do not need to activate it in each terminal. You can explore commands with:

bin/flask --help
bin/flask generate --help

If you used flask new store --skip-install, run bin/setup before continuing. Use that same setup command on a fresh checkout. Commit uv.lock so other developers and deployment builds use the same dependency versions. Never commit config/master.key.

items.title: A quick directory tour
items.text:
Open the generated directory in your editor:

Path Purpose app/models/ Data behavior, validations, and associations. app/controllers/ Actions that handle requests. app/views/ Jinja HTML and email templates. app/helpers/ Reusable template helpers. app/mailers/, app/jobs/ Email actions and background work. app/assets/ Stylesheets, images, and other source assets. config/routes.py URL-to-action mappings. config/database.yml Database connections by environment. config/environments/ Development, test, and production settings. db/migrate/ Database migration history. db/schema.py Generated snapshot of the migrated database. test/ Tests and fixtures. storage/ Local databases and uploaded files. bin/ Application commands and setup/release scripts. deploy/README.md Generated Docker and deployment instructions.

See Project structure for the complete layout.

items.title: Model, view, controller
items.text:
Most of our work will happen in three places:

  • A model represents application data and its rules: a Product, for example.
  • A controller handles a request, loads or changes data, and chooses a response.
  • A view turns the controller's data into HTML.

Routes connect a browser's request to the right controller action. We will build all of these pieces rather than start with a scaffold, so you can see how they fit together.

items.title: Hello, Flaskteroids!
items.text:
Start the development server:

bin/flask run --debug

Open http://127.0.0.1:5000. You should see the Flaskteroids welcome page. This confirms that the generated application boots and serves requests.

Keep the server in one terminal and run other commands in another terminal in store. Press Ctrl-C to stop the server. Debug mode reloads changed Python code and provides an interactive debugger; use it only on your own development machine.

Flaskteroids discovers components in their conventional directories. Python imports are still explicit: a controller imports the models it uses. After migrations, stop and restart the server so it loads the new schema snapshot.

items.title: Create a product model
items.text:
Stop the server and generate a model:

bin/flask generate model Product name:string description:text

This creates:

  • app/models/product.py: the behavioral model.
  • A migration under db/migrate/versions/: instructions for creating the table.
  • test/models/product_test.py: a starting point for model tests.

Use singular CamelCase for model names. Product maps to the plural table products by convention.

items.title: Understand the migration
items.text:
Open the generated migration. Its upgrade() function creates products with name and description columns, an integer primary key id, and timestamps created_at and updated_at. Its downgrade() function drops the table.

Migrations record structural changes so every environment can apply them in order. Review generated migrations before running them, especially when removing data or adding constraints.

Apply the migration:

bin/flask db:migrate

db:migrate applies pending migrations and regenerates db/schema.py. The application generator already prepared the development database. The generated database configuration uses storage/development.sqlite3 for development and a separate database for tests.

Open app/models/product.py:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    pass

An empty model is useful! Its mapped attributes come from the schema snapshot. We add application behavior here without repeating its column definitions.

Commit migrations and db/schema.py, but do not edit the snapshot by hand. Future database changes belong in new migrations. bin/flask db:rollback undoes the most recent migration; a rollback that drops data cannot recover that data.

items.title: Work with records in the shell
items.text:
Before building pages, let's see what a product can do. Open the application shell:

bin/flask shell

The shell provides an application context and makes your models available automatically. You can use Product directly. In the examples below, >>> is the Python prompt, not something to type; the lines without it show the result.

items.title: Create and query
items.text:
Build a product and save it:

>>> product = Product.new(name="T-Shirt", description="A comfortable cotton shirt.")
>>> product.save()
True
>>> product.name
'T-Shirt'

new() builds an unsaved object. save() validates and persists it, returning True on success. The database assigns product.id when the record is saved. Create another product with the combined build-and-save operation:

>>> pants = Product.create(name="Pants", description="Everyday trousers.")
>>> Product.count()
2
>>> [item.name for item in Product.all()]
['T-Shirt', 'Pants']

create() returns the object, including when validation fails. Later we will use its errors to explain unsuccessful saves.

Find and filter records:

>>> Product.find(product.id).name
'T-Shirt'
>>> Product.find_by(name="Pants").description
'Everyday trousers.'
>>> [item.name for item in Product.where(name="Pants").order(name="asc")]
['Pants']

find() raises RecordNotFoundException if the record is absent; find_by() returns None. all() and where() return lazy queries: iteration loads the records. Keep the returned query when chaining filters or ordering.

items.title: Update and delete
items.text:
Change the shirt's name, then try assigning and saving a description separately:

>>> product.update(name="Cotton T-Shirt")
True
>>> product.description = "Available in several colors."
>>> product.save()
True

Assignments alone do not save a record. A standalone save(), create(), update(), or destroy() commits before returning; no extra session or commit call is needed. See Models when several operations need to succeed together.

Create a temporary product and delete it:

>>> temporary = Product.create(name="Sample", description="For this example only.")
>>> temporary.destroy()
True
>>> Product.count()
2

The temporary record is gone, while our shirt and pants remain. We'll use those products when we build the catalog page.

items.title: Add validation
items.text:
A product without a name would be hard to browse. Exit the shell with exit(), then replace app/models/product.py with:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import validates


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    validates("name", presence=True)

Declarations such as validations, associations, and callbacks go directly inside the class body, with explicit imports. This validation requires a nonblank name. It changes behavior, not database structure, so there is no migration to run.

Open a new bin/flask shell to load the edited model:

>>> product = Product.new(name="", description="Still available for redisplay.")
>>> product.save()
False
>>> bool(product.errors)
True
>>> product.description
'Still available for redisplay.'

Run product.errors.full_messages() to read the validation messages. Notice that the object still holds the entered description. That will let us redisplay a form without making the visitor type everything again.

Fix the name and retry:

>>> product.name = "Socks"
>>> product.save()
True

Exit with exit(). Your development database now has three products: Cotton T-Shirt, Pants, and Socks. Next, let's give them a home on the web.

items.title: Follow a request through the application
items.text:
Our product data exists, but it has no web interface yet. A page request follows this path:

GET /products
  → config/routes.py
  → ProductsController.index()
  → Product.all()
  → app/views/products/index.html
  → HTML response

items.title: Define resource routes
items.text:
Replace config/routes.py with:

def register(route):
    route.get("/up/", to="flaskteroids/health#show")
    route.root(to="products#index")
    route.resources("products")

Keep the generated /up/ health route and the parameter name route, which other generators use when adding routes. The root route makes the catalog our home page. resources() creates the standard CRUD routes:

Method Path Action Purpose GET /products index List products. GET /products/new new Display a creation form. POST /products create Save a new product. GET /products/<int:id> show Display one product. GET /products/<int:id>/edit edit Display an editing form. PUT/PATCH /products/<int:id> update Save changes. DELETE /products/<int:id> destroy Delete a product.

GET retrieves information. POST creates it, PUT/PATCH updates it, and DELETE removes it. Helpers generate slashless resource URLs. A trailing slash is also accepted without redirecting or replaying a request body.

Inspect the application's routes with:

bin/flask routes

Routes identify actions with "controller#action": products#index means ProductsController.index. The framework discovers that class in app/controllers/products_controller.py.

items.title: Generate a controller
items.text:
bin/flask generate controller Products index --skip-routes

The generator creates a controller, helper, index template, and controller test. --skip-routes avoids adding routes because we already defined them.

Replace app/controllers/products_controller.py with:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.product import Product


class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    def index(self):
        self.products = Product.all()

When an action returns None, Flaskteroids renders its matching template. Controller instance variables become template variables: self.products is available as products.

Replace app/views/products/index.html with:

{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Products</h1>
  <ul>
    {% for product in products %}
      <li>{{ product.name }}</li>
    {% else %}
      <li>No products yet.</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
{% endblock %}

Jinja's {% ... %} tags control the template, while {{ ... }} outputs a value. The layout supplies the surrounding HTML; this template fills its body block. {% extends layout %} uses the framework-provided layout variable: normally layouts/application.html, or a minimal layout for Turbo Frame requests. Use this in page templates so they respect controller layout overrides and frame-aware layout selection.

Run bin/flask run --debug again and visit http://127.0.0.1:5000. You should see the products you created in the shell.

items.title: Build the CRUD interface
items.text: The catalog lists product names, but visitors cannot open a product yet. We'll add that first, then create products in the browser, edit them, and finally remove them. Keep the existing controller actions as you add each new one.

items.title: Show a product
items.text:
In app/controllers/products_controller.py, add a show action:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.product import Product


class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    def index(self):
        self.products = Product.all()

    def show(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])

The resource route captures the ID from /products/<int:id>. The show action finds that product and makes it available to its template as product.

Create app/views/products/show.html:

{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>{{ product.name }}</h1>
  <p>{{ product.description }}</p>
  {{ link_to("Back", products_path()) }}
{% endblock %}

Now give visitors a way to reach it. In app/views/products/index.html, replace <li>{{ product.name }}</li> with:

<li>{{ link_to(product.name, product_path(product)) }}</li>

link_to builds a link. Resource helpers such as product_path(product) have the same meaning in templates and Python; import them from flaskteroids.routes in Python code. Native Flask url_for remains available for custom endpoint-based routing.

Try it: refresh the catalog, click Cotton T-Shirt, and follow Back. You can now browse both the collection and an individual product without typing its ID.

items.title: Extract a presentation helper
items.text:
Move reusable presentation logic into app/helpers/products_helper.py. If the controller generator already created this file, replace its empty class:

class ProductsHelper:
    def product_link(self, product):
        return self.link_to(product.name, self.product_path(product))

In app/views/products/index.html, the product list item can now be:

<li>{{ product_link(product) }}</li>

Helper classes are loaded automatically: no controller import or callback is needed. Inside a helper, self provides the shared view context, including other helpers and route helpers. Ordinary strings are escaped; link_to returns safely constructed HTML. See application helpers for helper selection and inheritance.

items.title: Create products in the browser
items.text:
So far we have created products in the shell. A web form needs two actions: new displays it, and create processes its submission.

Add this import to the controller:

from flaskteroids.routes import product_path

Add these methods inside ProductsController, keeping index and show:

    def new(self):
        self.product = Product.new()

    def create(self):
        self.product = Product.new(**self._product_params())
        if self.product.save():
            return self.redirect_to(product_path(self.product))
        return self.render("new", status=422)

    def _product_params(self):
        return self.params.expect(product=["name", "description"])

Create app/views/products/new.html:

{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>New product</h1>
  {% call(form) form_with(model=product) %}
    {% if product.errors %}
      <ul class="errors">
        {% for message in product.errors.full_messages() %}
          <li>{{ message }}</li>
        {% endfor %}
      </ul>
    {% endif %}

    <div>
      {{ form.label("name") }}
      {{ form.text_field("name") }}
    </div>
    <div>
      {{ form.label("description") }}
      {{ form.text_area("description") }}
    </div>
    {{ form.submit("Save product") }}
  {% endcall %}
  {{ link_to("Cancel", products_path()) }}
{% endblock %}

form_with(model=product) chooses the creation URL, includes a CSRF token, and fills its inputs from the model. The generated field names put the submission inside a product object.

Our _product_params() method uses self.params.expect() to require that outer object and select only name and description. It does not require every listed field to be present. Never pass unfiltered request data to a model: visitors can submit attributes that your HTML form does not expose.

After the heading in app/views/products/index.html, add:

{{ link_to("New product", new_product_path()) }}

Try it: click New product and create a product named Hat. You should land on its show page. Follow Back and check that Hat appears in the catalog.

items.title: Help visitors correct mistakes
items.text:
Open New product again. Enter a description, leave the name blank, and save. You should stay on the form, see a validation message, and keep your description.

That happens because create renders new with status 422 when saving fails. Rendering reuses the invalid product, including its errors and entered values. A redirect would start a new request and lose that state.

Enter a name and save again. The same form now succeeds. We have connected the validation we tried in the shell to a useful browser experience.

items.title: Edit an existing product
items.text:
Editing has the same two-part shape: edit displays a form and update saves its submission. Add these methods to ProductsController:

    def edit(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])

    def update(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])
        if self.product.update(**self._product_params()):
            return self.redirect_to(product_path(self.product))
        return self.render("edit", status=422)

We could copy the creation form, but then every new field would need two edits. Instead, move the complete {% call(form) form_with(model=product) %} block, through its {% endcall %}, from new.html into a new file: app/views/products/_form.html.

The underscore marks this as a reusable partial. Replace new.html with:

{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>New product</h1>
  {% include "products/_form.html" %}
  {{ link_to("Cancel", products_path()) }}
{% endblock %}

Create app/views/products/edit.html:

{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Edit product</h1>
  {% include "products/_form.html" %}
  {{ link_to("Cancel", product_path(product)) }}
{% endblock %}

Both includes receive the current product. For a persisted record, form_with chooses its member URL and PATCH. The helper renders a POST form with a hidden PATCH override because browsers submit only GET or POST directly. An explicit method="PUT" is supported, but PATCH is the inferred update method.

After the Back link in app/views/products/show.html, add:

{{ link_to("Edit", edit_product_path(product)) }}

Try it: edit Hat, change its description, and save. Then try an edit with a blank name. The editing form should retain your changes and explain the error, just like the creation form. Correct the name before continuing.

items.title: Extract the repeated lookup
items.text:
show, edit, and update all start with the same product lookup. A before_action lets us run it once before any of those actions.

In app/controllers/products_controller.py, add this import alongside the existing imports:

from flaskteroids.actions import before_action

Add the declaration inside ProductsController, before its existing methods:

class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    before_action("_set_product", only=["show", "edit", "update"])

    # Keep the existing actions and private methods here.

Replace show, edit, and update with these methods, and add _set_product:

    def show(self):
        pass

    def edit(self):
        pass

    def update(self):
        if self.product.update(**self._product_params()):
            return self.redirect_to(product_path(self.product))
        return self.render("edit", status=422)

    def _set_product(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])

Keep index, new, create, and _product_params unchanged. Empty show and edit actions still render their matching templates; the callback supplies the record first.

Try it: visit a product and edit it again. The behavior should be identical; we have removed duplication without changing the interface.

items.title: Delete a product
items.text:
We can browse, create, and edit. The last CRUD operation is deletion.

Add products_path to the existing route-helper import:

from flaskteroids.routes import product_path, products_path

Add this action:

    def destroy(self):
        self.product.destroy()
        return self.redirect_to(products_path(), status=303)

Update the existing before_action call inside ProductsController to include destroy. Replace the call rather than adding a second one:

    before_action("_set_product", only=["show", "edit", "update", "destroy"])

After the Edit link in app/views/products/show.html, add a deletion button:

{{ button_to("Delete", product, method="DELETE") }}

This generates a POST form with a CSRF token and a hidden DELETE override. Deleting data is a state-changing operation, not a GET link. The controller redirects with status 303 so the browser retrieves the catalog afterward.

Try it: create a temporary product, delete it, and confirm that it disappears from the catalog. Keep the original products if you continue the tutorial.

You now have a complete CRUD interface. If you later add callbacks that can reject destruction, handle a False result from destroy() explicitly.

items.title: The scaffold shortcut
items.text:
You have built the pieces yourself so you can understand and customize them. For a future resource, a scaffold generates those pieces together. For example, in a separate application:

bin/flask generate scaffold Post title:string content:text
bin/flask db:migrate

Do not generate a Product scaffold over this tutorial: generators may overwrite your work.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
You have built a working catalog: visitors can browse products, create them, correct invalid input, edit details, and delete records.

Continue with Add login and product images to decide who can change the catalog. Or explore Models, Routing, and Forms to learn more about the pieces you have used.

items.title: Project structure
items.text:
Most application work happens in three places: app/ for behavior and templates, config/ for settings and routes, and db/ for database changes. flask new creates the layout below.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Find the files used by models, controllers, and views.
  • Recognize generated files and files you should commit.
  • Set up an existing application checkout.

items.text:

│   ├── assets/

items.title: Where to make changes
items.text: Path Contents app/assets Source stylesheets/images, served automatically in development/test. app/javascript Application JavaScript modules and entrypoints. vendor/javascript Downloaded, versioned JavaScript modules. config/importmap.py Logical JavaScript module mappings. bin/importmap Resolve, pin, and maintain downloaded JavaScript modules. public/assets Fingerprinted production assets and manifest, created by precompilation. app/controllers Request-handling actions. app/helpers Automatically loaded presentation helper classes. app/models Data rules and behavior: associations, validations, and callbacks. db/schema.py Generated column/table definitions. Commit this file; change the database through migrations, not by editing it. app/views Jinja templates. app/mailers Email actions. app/jobs Background jobs. config/application.py Application-wide configuration. config/environments Environment-specific overrides. config/initializers Library configuration that runs during boot. config/database.yml Database connections by environment. config/credentials.yml.enc Encrypted application secrets. config/routes.py Application routes. config/locales YAML translation catalogs. db/migrate Database migrations. storage Local database files and uploads; keep persistent in containers. bin/flask Run Flask commands using your app's environment. bin/jobs start Start a background job worker using your app's environment. bin/setup Install dependencies and prepare the database. bin/release migrate Apply database changes during deployment. bin/docker-entrypoint Start the Docker application. uv.lock Exact dependency versions; commit this file. deploy/README.md Your app's Docker and deployment guide. Procfile Example web and worker process commands. test Tests and YAML fixtures.

items.title: Set up an existing checkout
items.text:
A new app is ready to run. When you check out an existing project—or create one with --skip-install—run bin/setup to install its dependencies and prepare the database:

bin/setup

Next, explore Configuration to choose settings for each environment, or Assets to add styles and images.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Tests grow alongside your application. Generators give you starting tests for new features, and your new app includes a health check to get you going.

Run model, controller, job, and mailer tests as you work:

bin/flask test

Use browser tests to check the journey a person takes through your app:

bin/flask test:system

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Choose the right kind of test for a behavior.
  • Create fixture data and make requests in tests.
  • Check background work, email, and browser journeys.

items.title: Run a focused test
items.text:
Both commands use pytest, so you can select a file or run tests in parallel:

bin/flask test -n auto
bin/flask test test/controllers/posts_controller_test.py

The commands select the test environment and apply pending migrations. Tests that inherit from the framework's test classes roll back database changes after each test, so records from one test do not affect the next.

For upload tests, put example files in test/fixtures/files and use fixture_file_upload('avatar.png'). Uploads use temporary storage, leaving your real files untouched. See Attachments for examples.

items.title: Test types
items.text:
Import the base class you need from test.test_helper:

Base class What to test ModelTest Validations, queries, and model behavior IntegrationTest HTTP requests and responses JobTest Background work and enqueueing MailerTest Email content and delivery SystemTest User journeys in a real browser

Generated files end in _test.py, and test classes end in Test. Each base class provides an application context, fixture access, and the framework's assertions. Use ordinary pytest assertions alongside them.

items.title: Fixtures
items.text:
Fixtures live under test/fixtures:

# test/fixtures/posts.yml
one:
  title: First post
  content: First post content

two:
  title: Second post
  content: Second post content

Declare and access them from a test:

from test.test_helper import ModelTest


class PostTest(ModelTest):
    fixtures = ["posts"]

    def setup(self):
        self.post = self.posts("one")

    def test_fixture_has_a_title(self):
        assert self.post.title == "First post"

Each test gets its declared fixtures, and its changes are rolled back afterward. Use fixture labels rather than hard-coded IDs; generated IDs may have gaps.

items.title: Integration tests
items.text:
Make requests without starting a web server, then check the response or the resulting database change:

from test.test_helper import IntegrationTest, get, post
from app.models.post import Post
from flaskteroids.routes import post_url, posts_url


class PostsControllerTest(IntegrationTest):
    fixtures = ["posts"]

    def test_index_returns_success(self):
        get(posts_url())
        self.assert_response("success")

    def test_create_saves_post(self):
        with self.assert_difference(Post.count):
            post(
                posts_url(),
                params={"post": {"title": "New post", "content": "Content"}},
            )

        self.assert_redirected_to(post_url(Post.last()))

Available request functions are get, post, patch, put, and delete.

items.title: State changes
items.text:
Use assert_changes around an operation to check that an expression changes:

with self.assert_changes(lambda: post.title, was="Draft", to="Published"):
    post.update(title="Published")

was checks the value before the block, and to checks the value afterward. Both are optional; the expression must change even when neither is supplied.

items.title: Jobs and mail
items.text:
The test environment keeps queued jobs and delivered email in memory. Inside a test method, use these helpers with your job and mailer classes:

with self.assert_enqueued_with(job=PublishPostJob, kwargs={"post_id": post.id}):
    PublishPostJob().perform_later(post_id=post.id)

with self.perform_enqueued_jobs():
    PublishPostJob().perform_later(post_id=post.id)

with self.assert_emails(1):
    PostsMailer.published(post).deliver_now()

assert_enqueued_with checks that a job was scheduled. perform_enqueued_jobs runs jobs enqueued inside its block. assert_emails checks how many messages were delivered. Built messages are available through self.deliveries as EmailMessage objects, so tests can inspect headers and HTML/plain-text parts. No broker or SMTP server is required.

To inspect email appearance interactively, use mailer previews. Previews render example emails in the development browser without delivery; they complement automated tests rather than replacing them.

items.title: System tests
items.text:
System tests use Playwright through helpers such as visit and assert_selector. Chromium is started lazily and reused within each system-test class. Every test gets a fresh browser context and page, so cookies, local storage, and browser handlers do not carry over between tests. Playwright stops after the class so unrelated tests can use their own asyncio event loops. Database changes and uploaded files remain isolated by the normal test lifecycle.

For example:

from test.test_helper import SystemTest
from flaskteroids.routes import posts_path


class PostsTest(SystemTest):
    def test_index_shows_posts_heading(self):
        self.visit(posts_path())
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="Posts")

Fill fields by their labels, supplying the contents through value:

self.fill_in("Title", value="First post")
self.fill_in_rich_text_area("Content", value="<div>Hello</div>")

Rich-text values are HTML, loaded through Lexxy's public value property. See Rich text for setup and model fixtures.

items.title: Install the browser
items.text:
Flaskteroids includes the Playwright Python package, but not the browser itself. Install Chromium before running your first system test:

.venv/bin/playwright install chromium

items.title: Writing Flaskteroids guides
items.text:
A guide helps someone understand a feature and use it in an application. It is not an inventory of every method, option, exception, or implementation detail.

This approach takes inspiration from the Rails Guides, especially Getting Started, Active Record Basics, and the Guides Guidelines. Borrow their teaching structure, not claims that Flaskteroids implements every Rails feature.

items.title: Start with the reader's goal
items.text:
Open with the problem the feature solves, followed by a short list of what the reader will learn. State prerequisites and the starting application state before the first example.

Choose one kind of page:

  • Tutorial: build a feature step by step in a named application. Each step depends on the ones before it.
  • Component guide: explain a feature through a small, coherent example. Readers should not have to complete the whole store tutorial first.

Keep exhaustive signatures, option tables, backend internals, and extension contracts for separate API documentation.

items.title: Teach one workflow at a time
items.text:
Introduce the simplest useful path first:

  1. Explain what the reader is about to do and why.
  2. Show the command or code, including its file path.
  3. Explain the result and how to check it.
  4. Add alternatives only after the basic workflow works.

Keep related steps together. A form example should lead to permitted parameters, saving, and validation redisplay before discussing unrelated helper options. A mailer example should reach a local preview before requiring SMTP setup.

Split a page when it starts teaching a separate feature. Link to the focused guide instead of repeating its installation steps or configuration catalog.

items.title: Write directly and calmly
items.text:
Address the reader as “you.” Use “we” when walking through a tutorial together. Prefer short paragraphs, active sentences, and familiar words.

Lead with application behavior:

  • Prefer “Assigning a value does not save it” over “Scalar publication is staged.”
  • Prefer “If saving fails, render the submitted object again” over “The input graph retains rejected state.”
  • Explain a term such as “partial” before showing several ways to call it.

Use sentence-case headings that describe a task or concept. Avoid headings such as “Advanced” that do not tell readers what they will find.

items.title: Make examples usable
items.text:
Use one set of domain names within a guide. Show imports at module scope, and identify the file being edited. Say whether a snippet replaces a class, adds a method, or changes an existing declaration.

Run application commands with bin/flask from the application root. Use flask new before the application exists. Explain any additional tools, worker processes, migrations, or server restarts when they become necessary.

Do not include terminal prompt characters in copyable shell commands. Use pycon for interactive Python examples with prompts and results.

Keep examples focused on the step being taught. A small table can clarify a choice; a catalog of every supported option belongs in API documentation.

items.title: Keep important boundaries close
items.text:
Do not remove a warning merely to shorten a guide. Explain safety and correctness where the reader needs them: permitted parameters beside assignment, CSRF beside form submission, download authorization beside file links, and after-commit delivery beside background email.

Describe intentional limitations in terms of the reader's task. Distinguish what works from what the application must supply. Do not imply full Rails parity from a shared method name, or require SQLAlchemy session knowledge for ordinary work.

items.title: Review a guide
items.text:
Before publishing, check:

  • Can a reader identify the goal and starting point from the introduction?
  • Does each example introduce one idea and explain its result?
  • Does the main workflow work without following an advanced detour?
  • Are failures, security boundaries, and unsupported behavior clear?
  • Do moved sections have updated links and navigation?
  • Does the page end with a useful next step rather than another option list?

items.title: Preview and build the site
items.text:
The guides use Zensical with its classic theme. From the repository root, install the locked documentation tools:

uv sync --locked --group docs

Preview changes locally:

uv run --locked --group docs zensical serve

After editing links or navigation in zensical.toml, run the strict build used by CI:

uv run --locked --group docs zensical build --strict --clean

The generated site is written to site/. The documentation workflow publishes it to the existing gh-pages branch after a release or a manual run. GitHub Pages should continue serving the root of that branch.

items.title: Controllers
items.text:
Controllers handle HTTP requests. Each action is a public method on a controller class. Actions load or change model data, then render a page, return JSON, or redirect the browser.

This guide uses browser controllers (Controller). For an application that serves data without browser views, see Building an API.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Write an action and pass data to its view.
  • Render responses, redirect, and accept permitted input.
  • Share request behavior with controller callbacks.

items.title: Write an action
items.text:
If an action does not prepare a response, Flaskteroids renders its matching template. Instance variables become template variables:

# app/controllers/posts_controller.py
from app.models.post import Post
from flaskteroids.controller import Controller


class PostsController(Controller):
    def index(self):
        self.posts = Post.all()

    def show(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])

index renders app/views/posts/index.html, where posts is available. show renders app/views/posts/show.html, where post is available. Native Flask response return values, including empty strings and dictionaries, are also supported.

Read request input from self.params. Templates can access the same mapping as params. Before passing input to a model, filter it with self.params.expect(...).

items.title: Rendering responses
items.text:
Use render when you need to choose the template, response format, or status:

return self.render("new", status=422)
return self.render(json={"message": "Saved"}, status=200)

self.render() without a template name selects the current action. Status values can be integers or HTTPStatus members.

Rendering prepares a response; it does not stop Python execution. Use return self.render(...) to exit the action. Preparing another response raises DoubleRenderError from flaskteroids.exceptions.

The template/helper function render(...) is different: it renders a record, partial, or exact template to HTML, not a controller response. See view rendering.

items.title: JSON values
items.text:
Pass a model, query, or ordinary JSON value to render(json=...). Models use their __json__() method to choose the attributes in the response. You can also combine records and queries inside a dictionary:

return self.render(json={"posts": Post.all(), "featured": post})

Model errors become the list returned by errors.full_messages():

return self.render(json=post.errors, status=422)
# Example body: ["Field title is blank"]

An empty error collection becomes []. Scaffold create/update actions use this format for JSON validation failures. See model serialization for field selection and authentication-secret filtering.

items.title: Turbo Frames and Stream responses
items.text:
Controllers expose self.turbo_frame_request (boolean) and self.turbo_frame_request_id (ID or None). Page views using {% extends layout %} select layout = "layouts/application.html" normally and frame_layout = "layouts/turbo/frame.html" for frame requests. Override either path on the controller class or instance before rendering.

Use self.render(turbo_stream=self.turbo_stream.remove(self.post)) for an HTTP Stream response, or pass a list/tuple of operations. Templates can use the conventional <action>.turbo_stream.html name. See Turbo Frames and Streams for examples, HTML fallback, and representation-specific cache validators.

items.title: Headers and response state
items.text:
Set response headers before rendering:

self.response.headers["X-Report-Version"] = "1"
return self.render(json={"ready": True})

Setting a header does not prepare a response body. You can still render, redirect, or return an empty response afterward.

items.title: Redirects and empty responses
items.text:
return self.redirect_to(product_path(product), notice="Saved")
return self.redirect_to(products_path(), status=303, alert="Product removed")
return self.head(204, headers={"X-Result": "complete"})

Use status 303 See Other after successful Turbo form mutations, and render invalid HTML forms with 422 so Turbo can redisplay validation errors.

Redirects can include a notice or alert. head prepares an empty response. Both use the same response tracking as render and respond_to.

As with rendering, return their result when the action should stop. In a before callback, preparing a response stops the callback chain even without a return.

items.title: Content negotiation
items.text:
Use respond_to to serve HTML, JSON, or Turbo Streams from the same action:

from app.models.post import Post
from flaskteroids.controller import Controller


class PostsController(Controller):
    def index(self):
        self.posts = Post.all()
        self.respond_to(
            html=lambda: self.render("index"),
            json=lambda: self.render(json=self.posts),
        )

A resource URL's .json or .turbo_stream suffix takes precedence over the Accept header. Without either, HTML is selected. A requested format you do not offer returns 406 Not Acceptable.

Add a turbo_stream=lambda: self.render() handler to use a conventional Stream template. Ordinary Turbo forms can fall back to offered HTML. See Stream negotiation for template fallback and forced-format URLs.

The selected response is recorded on the controller, so returning it is optional. HTML handlers can leave template rendering implicit. JSON handlers must render or return a response.

items.title: Controller callbacks
items.text:
Use callbacks for work shared by several actions, such as loading a record or checking authentication:

from app.models.post import Post
from flaskteroids.actions import before_action
from flaskteroids.controller import Controller


class PostsController(Controller):
    before_action("_set_post", only=["show", "edit", "update", "destroy"])

    def show(self):
        pass  # The callback has loaded self.post; render show.html.

    def _set_post(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])

Import declarations explicitly and call them inside the class. Controllers use the same declaration rules as models and mailers, including inheritance through ordinary mixins.

items.title: Inherited actions
items.text: Child controllers inherit actions and callbacks. A callback without only also covers actions added by the child. Calling super().action() runs the parent action and its callbacks. Mailers follow the same rules.

items.title: Around and after callbacks
items.text:
An around_action method is a generator: setup runs before yield, and cleanup runs after it. Yield exactly once to run the action:

from time import monotonic

from app.models.post import Post
from flask import current_app
from flaskteroids.actions import around_action
from flaskteroids.controller import Controller


class PostsController(Controller):
    around_action("_log_duration")

    def index(self):
        self.posts = Post.all()

    def _log_duration(self):
        started = monotonic()
        yield
        current_app.logger.info("Action duration: %.3fs", monotonic() - started)

On a successful request, the order is:

  1. Before callbacks, in declaration order.
  2. Around callback setup, in declaration order.
  3. The action and any implicit template rendering.
  4. Around cleanup, in reverse order.
  5. After callbacks, in declaration order.

After callbacks can edit self.response, but cannot prepare a second response.

items.title: Stopping callbacks and handling failures
items.text:
A before callback that prepares or returns a response stops the chain. Use this for checks such as requiring login: redirecting to the login page prevents the protected action from running.

An around callback must yield exactly once to run the action. Returning before the yield skips it. Entered around callbacks still clean up if the action fails; after callbacks run only when the action and cleanup succeed.

items.title: Controller helpers
items.text:
Presentation helper classes in app/helpers/*_helper.py are automatically available to views. Their methods run on the view context, not the controller. Use helper(...) to include extra classes when automatic inclusion is restricted.

To expose a method that needs controller state, use helper_method:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from flaskteroids.controller import helper_method


class PostsController(ApplicationController):
    helper_method("_display_name")

    def _display_name(self, post):
        return post.title or "Untitled"

Call it in a template, layout, or partial:

{{ display_name(post) }}

The template name drops the leading underscore by default. Set name="another_name" to choose a different name. These helpers are inherited, use the current controller, and remain private methods rather than routable actions. Other private methods are not exposed. Return ordinary strings for text that should be HTML-escaped.

Mailers provide the same declaration through flaskteroids.mailer.helper_method, but delegate to the mailer's state. See mailer helpers.

The authentication generator exposes is_authenticated() this way. It resumes the session on demand, so public pages can show login/logout controls without an extra callback. Calling it does not require login; _require_authentication enforces access control.

items.title: Rate limits
items.text:
Use a rate limit to reject requests when a client sends too many in a short period. For example, you can limit repeated requests to a public endpoint.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Add a request limit to a controller.
  • Recognize the response when the limit is exceeded.
  • Account for process-local counters in a deployment.

items.title: Add a limit
items.text:
Declare the limit inside the controller class:

from flaskteroids.controller import Controller
from flaskteroids.rate_limit import rate_limit


class StatusController(Controller):
    rate_limit(to=5, within=60)

    def index(self):
        return self.head(200)

This allows five requests per client IP within 60 seconds. Exceeding the limit returns 429 Too Many Requests. Use only=["index"] to apply a limit to selected actions rather than the whole controller.

To customize the rejection response, pass a controller method name through using, for example using="_rate_limit_exceeded", and return a response from that method.

items.title: Default cache
items.text:
Each application has its own counters. The default cache is in memory and is not shared between worker processes. Values disappear when the process ends.

These are not deployment-wide limits. For a multi-process deployment, choose an appropriate shared rate-limiting solution at your proxy or infrastructure layer rather than assuming these counters protect all workers together.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: See Controller callbacks to share other request checks across actions.

items.title: Building an API
items.text:
Use an API-only application when your clients need data rather than server-rendered pages—for example, a mobile app or a separate JavaScript frontend. You still use Flaskteroids models, routes, controllers, jobs, and mailers, but return JSON instead of rendering browser views.

This guide builds a small posts API. If you have not installed Flaskteroids yet, follow the installation steps first.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Generate an API-only application.
  • Accept JSON input and return records or validation errors.
  • Test requests without a browser.

items.title: Create the application
items.text:
flask new blog --api
cd blog

The generator installs dependencies and prepares the development database. Run application commands with bin/flask; no environment activation is needed.

Generate a resource and apply its migration:

bin/flask generate scaffold Post title:string content:text
bin/flask db:migrate
bin/flask run

The scaffold creates a model, migration, routes, controller, and request tests. It does not create HTML views or forms.

items.title: Make a request
items.text:
In another terminal, create a post:

curl -i http://127.0.0.1:5000/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"post": {"title": "Hello", "content": "My first post."}}'

The response has status 201 Created, the saved post as JSON, and a Location header pointing to its URL. Fetch the collection with:

curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/posts

The generated resource supports these requests:

Method Path Result on success GET /posts 200 with a JSON array of posts GET /posts/<id> 200 with one post POST /posts 201 with the created post and a Location header PATCH/PUT /posts/<id> 200 with the updated post DELETE /posts/<id> 204 with an empty body

There are no new or edit pages: the client supplies the interface. Resource routes omit those actions unless explicitly requested with only. Nested and singular resources follow the same convention. Resource helpers accept format="json"; API-only applications do not add Turbo Stream routes.

Visit /posts, not /: an application without a root route returns 404 rather than a welcome page.

items.title: Work with controllers
items.text:
Open app/controllers/application_controller.py:

from flaskteroids.controller import APIController


class ApplicationController(APIController):
    pass

Your controllers inherit from this base. They use the same callbacks, strong parameters, model serialization, headers, localization, and redirects as browser controllers. The difference is the default response: an action that neither renders nor returns a response sends 204 No Content, rather than looking for a template.

The scaffold's create action builds a post from permitted input, saves it, and renders either the record or its validation errors:

    def create(self):
        self.post = Post.new(**self._post_params())
        if self.post.save():
            return self.render(json=self.post, status=201, location=self.post)
        return self.render(json=self.post.errors, status=422)

    def _post_params(self):
        return self.params.expect(post=["title", "content"])

location= accepts a URL string, a saved model, or a nested model sequence. Models resolve to a relative resource URL. Models and queries use the framework's JSON serialization; validation errors become a list of full messages. Rejected saves and destructions return 422 in scaffold actions.

Use self.head(status) for an empty response, or return an ordinary Flask response for files and plain text. API-only does not mean JSON-only, and explicit JSON rendering does not require an Accept header. As with browser controllers, prepare only one response per action.

You can also use APIController in an application that serves browser pages. It does not change the behavior of other controllers using Controller.

items.title: Accept JSON input
items.text:
JSON request bodies populate self.params. Both of these bodies work with self.params.expect(post=["title"]):

{"post": {"title": "Hello"}}

{"title": "Hello"}

By convention, the controller wraps unwrapped input under its model name while retaining the original values. An existing root is never replaced. When a conventional model exists, wrapping selects mapped columns and writable framework attributes. Wrapping does not permit attributes for assignment: always filter input with strong parameters.

To customize wrapping, declare it inside the controller class:

from flaskteroids.controller import APIController, wrap_parameters


class EventsController(APIController):
    wrap_parameters(False)

Use wrap_parameters("event") for a custom root, or wrap_parameters(True) to restore conventional wrapping. Subclasses inherit the declaration and can override it independently. Forms and multipart uploads keep their usual parameter conventions.

Request parsing also accepts application/*+json. Body values are merged with query parameters, then path parameters; later sources take precedence. Non-object JSON is available under self.params["_json"]. Malformed JSON returns 400.

For JSON database columns, scaffold fields such as settings:json use the explicit JSONValue parameter schema. This preserves nested objects, arrays, scalars, and null while other fields remain allowlisted independently. See JSON-valued fields.

items.title: Test the API
items.text:
Run the generated request tests:

bin/flask test

No browser is required. Add behavior-focused tests using the same request helpers as a browser application, passing request bodies with json=:

from test.test_helper import IntegrationTest, post


class PostsAPITest(IntegrationTest):
    def test_create_returns_saved_post(self):
        response = post("/posts", json={"post": {"title": "Hello"}})

        assert response.status_code == 201
        assert response.get_json()["title"] == "Hello"

Framework HTTP errors return JSON with error and status fields, preserving headers such as Retry-After and WWW-Authenticate. Production errors do not expose internal exception details; configured exception propagation remains available for debugging. Validation errors rendered by your actions keep their own representation. See Testing for fixtures and request helpers.

items.title: Application defaults and authentication
items.text:
The generated app sets config.api_only = True in config/application.py. This selects application facilities, routing defaults, and generator output at initialization; controller inheritance determines response behavior.

Models, migrations, jobs, mailers, translations, and file storage remain available, including mailer templates and helpers. Browser views, application helpers, assets, Turbo, and system tests are omitted. Generated CI does not install a browser, and Docker builds do not precompile assets.

API requests are stateless by default. Cookie sessions, flash, browser form method override, and the session-bound rich-text editor upload endpoint are not installed. Stateless API controllers do not require browser CSRF tokens. Browser controllers retain CSRF protection, even inside an API-only app.

The authentication generator builds a browser login workflow and cannot be used in an API-only application. Cookie-session opt-ins, JWT, OAuth, and OpenAPI are not built in. Choose an authentication approach appropriate for your clients; do not enable cookie authentication by merely disabling CSRF protection.

items.title: Routing
items.text:
Routes connect URLs and HTTP methods to controller actions. Define them in config/routes.py, inside its register(route) function.

A destination such as "products#show" means: call show on ProductsController in app/controllers/products_controller.py.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Connect a URL to a controller action.
  • Declare resource routes and nested resources.
  • Generate paths in Python and templates.

items.title: Individual routes
items.text:
def register(route):
    route.root(to="products#index")
    route.get("/about", to="pages#about", aka="about")
    route.post("/login", to="sessions#create")
    route.put("/products/<int:id>", to="products#update")
    route.patch("/products/<int:id>", to="products#update")
    route.delete("/products/<int:id>", to="products#destroy")

<int:id> captures an integer from the URL and makes it available as self.params["id"]. Other bindings use Flask/Werkzeug's converter syntax.

The root route controls /. If you omit it, Flaskteroids shows its welcome page. Individual routes keep the trailing-slash spelling you declare.

items.title: Resources
items.text:
Use resources for the standard create, read, update, and delete actions:

def register(route):
    route.resources("products")
Method Path Action Public path helper GET /products index products_path() POST /products create products_path() GET /products/new new new_product_path() GET /products/<int:id> show product_path(product) GET /products/<int:id>/edit edit edit_product_path(product) PUT/PATCH /products/<int:id> update product_path(product) DELETE /products/<int:id> destroy product_path(product)

A collection URL addresses all products; a member URL addresses one. Several actions share a path: the HTTP method selects which action runs. For example, GET /products lists products, while POST /products creates one.

Resource helpers generate paths without trailing slashes. Requests with or without a trailing slash reach the same action, including .json/ and .turbo_stream/ requests.

Limit actions with only; an empty list generates no resource actions:

route.resources("products", only=["create", "update", "destroy"])

Collection and member helpers remain available even if you exclude index/show. Unsupported HTTP methods on framework routes return 404; they do not run another action as a fallback.

items.title: Uncountable resources
items.text:
Uncountable names distinguish collection and member helpers with _index:

route.resources("fish")

fish_index_path()  # /fish
fish_path(fish)    # /fish/1
new_fish_path()    # /fish/new

Model-backed forms and buttons use these same names, including nested resources.

items.title: Singular resources
items.text:
A singular resource has no member ID:

route.resource("session", only=["new", "create", "destroy"])

This provides new_session_path() at /session/new and session_path() at /session. POST creates a session; DELETE destroys it. The controller remains plural: SessionsController. A default singular resource additionally provides show, edit, and PUT/PATCH update, but never index.

items.title: Nested resources
items.text:
Nest a resource when its URL should include a parent, such as a product's subscribers:

route.resources(
    "products",
    nested=lambda child: child.resources("subscribers"),
)

The parent's own member routes still receive id. A subscriber collection receives product_id; a subscriber member receives both product_id and its own id.

products_path()                              # /products
product_path(product)                        # /products/1
product_subscribers_path(product)            # /products/1/subscribers
product_subscriber_path(product, subscriber) # /products/1/subscribers/2
new_product_subscriber_path(product)         # /products/1/subscribers/new
edit_product_subscriber_path(product, subscriber)
# /products/1/subscribers/2/edit

Deeper nesting keeps every ancestor's identifier. To declare several child resources, unpack their returned route lists:

route.resources("products", nested=lambda child: [
    *child.resources("subscribers"),
    *child.resources("reviews"),
])

items.title: Custom parameters
items.text:
route.resources(
    "products", param="slug",
    nested=lambda child: child.resources("subscribers"),
)

The parent receives slug; the child receives product_slug plus its own id. param="int:sku" instead supplies integer sku and product_sku bindings. Path bindings take precedence over query parameters and form fields. Setting param="slug" changes the URL parameter name; it does not tell helpers to read product.slug. Pass the slug explicitly, or override to_param():

product_path("cotton-shirt")
product_subscriber_path(product_slug="cotton-shirt", id=2)

class Product(ApplicationModel):
    def to_param(self):
        return self.slug if self.is_persisted() else None

The default to_param() returns a persisted record's ID as a string; unsaved records have no member identity. Model-backed forms/buttons for new records use collection destinations instead.

items.title: Helpers in Python and templates
items.text:
from flaskteroids.routes import product_path, product_url

product_path(product)               # /products/1
product_path(id=1, page=2)           # /products/1?page=2
product_url(product)                # https://example.test/products/1

The same helpers are available directly in Jinja:

{{ link_to(product.name, product_path(product)) }}

Every _path helper has a _url counterpart that includes the scheme and host. Helpers use the active application's routes and deployment prefix. They do not query records or fill missing parameters from the current request.

Supply each path parameter explicitly, using a saved record or its identifier. Missing or duplicate parameters raise an error rather than producing an incomplete URL.

For absolute links outside a request, such as links in email, use an application context and configure Flask's SERVER_NAME. Deployments with a URL prefix or a specific scheme may also need APPLICATION_ROOT and PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME. Do not forward unfiltered request parameters to URL helpers.

An individual route's aka declares its public helper name:

route.get("/dashboard", to="products#index", aka="dashboard")
# dashboard_path(), dashboard_url()

items.title: Response formats
items.text:
Use resource format suffixes, not separate action helpers:

products_path(format="json")        # /products.json
product_path(product, format="json") # /products/1.json
products_path(format="turbo_stream") # /products.turbo_stream
product_path(product, format="turbo_stream") # /products/1.turbo_stream

These URLs call the same actions as the HTML paths. Use self.respond_to(...) in the controller to choose an HTML, JSON, or Turbo Stream response. Explicit .json and .turbo_stream suffixes override Accept negotiation; .turbo_stream forces a Stream response, not HTML fallback. Without a suffix, Turbo forms can negotiate Streams or fall back to acceptable HTML. See Turbo Streams.

Suffix support belongs to resource routes. Existing custom named routes do not automatically gain .json or .turbo_stream variants.

items.title: HTML method overrides
items.text:
Browsers submit GET or POST forms. form_with and button_to render PUT/PATCH/DELETE as POST plus a hidden _method and a CSRF token:

{{ button_to("Log out", session_path(), method="DELETE") }}

Use the helpers rather than building hidden fields yourself. An overridden DELETE has the same routing and CSRF protection as an actual DELETE request. Overrides apply to all routes in the application, including native Flask routes; request.method reports the effective method.

For manual requests:

  • Only POST can be overridden.
  • The _method form field takes precedence over X-HTTP-Method-Override.
  • Query parameters cannot change the method.
  • An unsupported override leaves the request as POST.

items.title: Model basics
items.text:
Models represent your application's data and the rules for working with it. Use them to query records, validate input, manage associations, and save changes.

Define columns in database migrations and behavior in model classes. Flaskteroids reads column definitions from the generated db/schema.py; you do not repeat them in your models. SQLAlchemy is available for advanced queries and integration, but ordinary model work does not require managing a session.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Generate a model and apply its database migration.
  • Create, find, update, and delete records.
  • Handle invalid input and group saves in a transaction.

The examples use an Author and its Post records. Run commands from your application root. If you are new to Flaskteroids, start with Getting started.

items.title: Define models and migrate
items.text:
Application models inherit from the generated abstract base:

# app/models/application_model.py
from flaskteroids.model import Model


class ApplicationModel(Model):
    __abstract__ = True

Generate models and their migrations from your application directory:

bin/flask generate model Author name:string
bin/flask generate model Post title:string author:references
bin/flask db:prepare

Add behavior to the generated classes:

# app/models/author.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_many, validates


class Author(ApplicationModel):
    has_many("posts", dependent="destroy")
    validates("name", presence=True)

    def greeting(self):
        return f"Hello, {self.name}"

# app/models/post.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import belongs_to, validates


class Post(ApplicationModel):
    belongs_to("author")
    validates("title", presence=True)

Post uses the posts table by convention. Set __table_name__ = "legacy_posts" to use a different table.

items.title: The schema snapshot
items.text:
Successful db:migrate, db:prepare, and db:rollback commands regenerate db/schema.py from the selected database. Commit the snapshot, but do not edit it by hand. To refresh it without migrating, run bin/flask db:schema:dump. Restart servers and workers after migrations so they load the new definitions. See database commands.

The snapshot describes tables, columns, keys, constraints, indexes, and server defaults, including tables with no model class. It does not contain validations, associations, or other model behavior.

items.title: Queries
items.text:
Use find() when you have a record's ID:

post = Post.find(1)

If the record is absent, find() raises RecordNotFoundException. To look up a record by an attribute and receive None when it is absent, use find_by():

post = Post.find_by(title="First")

items.title: Filter and order records
items.text:
Build a query with where(), then add ordering or pagination:

posts = Post.where(title="First")
page = posts.order(title="asc").limit(20).offset(40)
for post in page:
    print(post.title)

Queries are lazy: iteration loads the records. Methods such as first() and count() also run the query. all() returns a query, not a list; use list(Post.all()) when you need a list.

Queries return new scopes rather than changing the original query. Keep the result when you add a filter or ordering. Iterating again runs the query again.

By default, records are ordered by ascending primary key. Limits and offsets apply to count() too. For an expression-based filter, use model attributes:

posts = Post.where(Post.title.ilike("a%"))

To preload related records, see Load associations together.
