items.title: Assignment, validation, and persistence
items.text:
Build a record, then check the result of saving it:

author = Author.create(name="Ada")
post = Post.new(title="First", author=author)
if post.save():
    identifier = post.id
else:
    messages = post.errors.full_messages()

create() builds and saves in one call. It returns the record even if validation fails. update() assigns attributes and returns whether saving succeeded:

post = Post.create(title="", author=author)
assert post.errors
assert post.update(title="Fixed")

items.title: Unsaved changes
items.text:
Assigning a scalar attribute changes what you read on that object, but does not save it to the database until a successful save. Invalid input and its errors remain available for correction and form redisplay. Another object's save or a later commit does not accidentally save these edits. This also applies to valid edits you have not explicitly saved.

  • reload() loads saved state and discards pending scalar input and errors.
  • discard_changes() discards pending scalar input without refreshing saved state.

items.title: Validate records
items.text:
Validations express rules that input must satisfy before a record can be saved. For example, update the title validation in app/models/post.py:

    validates("title", presence=True, length={"minimum": 3, "maximum": 100})

Keep the existing imports and association declaration. Now a blank or overly short title prevents saving. You can also check a record without saving it:

post = Post.new(title="", author=author)
if not post.is_valid():
    messages = post.errors.full_messages()

The record keeps its submitted input and errors. Correct the input and save again, or render the same object in a form so the user can correct it. See Forms.

Converting input to a column type is not validation. For numeric input, use a numericality validation to reject malformed values rather than relying on conversion alone. See Fields.

items.title: Defaults
items.text:
Put persistent defaults in migrations. Simple literal database defaults are available on new objects without a query. Database functions, computed columns, and generated IDs become available when the database writes the record. Explicit None does not request a default; JSON retains its native JSON-null behavior.

save() maintains declared created_at and updated_at attributes. Native writes do not run this timestamp behavior automatically.

Python default functions cannot be recovered from the database snapshot. Use assignment or initialization callbacks for application-side defaults, rather than Column.default definitions or edits to db/schema.py.

items.title: Transactions
items.text:
A standalone save(), create(), or update() commits before returning. Associated rows saved by the operation share its transaction. A failure or halted callback rolls back that operation, not earlier successful standalone saves.

Use an explicit transaction when several operations must succeed together:

with Author.transaction():
    author = Author.create(name="Ada")
    post = Post.create(title="First", author=author)
    if post.errors:
        raise ValueError("Post is invalid")
# Both writes commit here; an exception escaping the block rolls both back.

Saves inside the block join its transaction without committing individually. A False save result does not abort the block; raise an exception when the whole group should roll back. Transactions cover all models in the application, not just the class used to open the block.

Nested Model.transaction() blocks join the outer transaction by default. Use requires_new=True for a savepoint. Catch a failure outside the inner block if the outer operation should continue. After-commit callbacks wait for the outer commit, not savepoint release.

save(validate=False) skips validation, not database constraints. Integrity errors propagate as exceptions rather than model errors. Standalone failures clean up their transaction. After a database error inside an explicit transaction, roll back/recover that transaction before further writes. An earlier query does not turn a later standalone save into an explicit transaction.

items.title: Delete records
items.text:
Call destroy() to delete a record:

post = Post.find(1)
if post.destroy():
    print("Post removed")

Destruction runs callbacks and commits before returning, unless it joins an explicit transaction. A callback can reject it: destroy() then returns False and rolls back that standalone operation. Inside a transaction, raise an exception if rejection should roll back the whole group.

For deleting related records, see Association deletion.

items.title: Associations
items.text:
A model can belong to another record or have a collection of related records. For example, an author has many posts, and each post belongs to an author.

Read Model associations to declare relationships, build records through them, and save related form input.

items.title: Callbacks
items.text: Use callbacks for behavior that should run whenever a model is saved or destroyed. Use after_commit for external work, such as scheduling email after a successful save. See Model callbacks for examples.

items.title: Passwords
items.text:
Use the authentication generator for a complete login and password-reset workflow. It sets up has_secure_password() so the database stores a digest, not a plaintext password.

Follow Add login and product images for a walkthrough. Do not log password input, digests, or reset tokens.

items.title: Encrypted attributes
items.text:
Use encrypts("notes") for randomized string/text encryption. Use encrypts("email", deterministic=True, downcase=True) when equality lookups are needed. Assignment, validations, and forms still work with plaintext; database storage uses ciphertext.

Rich-text encryption uses the same service and dedicated keys. See Attribute encryption for setup, queries, key rotation, and limits.

items.title: Temporary attributes and serialization
items.text:
For a value that should not be saved, declare a class default, a property with a setter, or a private cache name. Initialize mutable caches per instance. Unknown public assignments raise AttributeError, and framework methods/metadata cannot be replaced through assignment.

Temporary values are not automatically saved or serialized. Repeated lookups in one session return the same object, including its temporary state.

Default JSON includes mapped scalar attributes and staged values, but excludes authentication secrets and virtual fields. Override __json__() for a custom response, or add names to the _serialization_exclude set. Form values are independent of JSON serialization. Ordinary editors/type checkers generally cannot infer dynamically mapped fields.

items.title: Class-body declarations
items.text: Import declarations such as validates, belongs_to, and before_save at module scope, then call them directly inside the model class. Callbacks can name methods defined later in that class. Put shared declarations in an abstract base model or a mixin.

items.title: Native SQLAlchemy and transactions
items.text:
SQLAlchemy is available for advanced queries and integrations. Ordinary model work should use the framework's query and persistence methods.

Native and bulk writes bypass framework validations and save callbacks. They also need an explicit transaction or commit; leaving an application context rolls back unfinished native work. A framework save can flush native pending changes, so use explicit transaction boundaries when mixing the two APIs.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Model associations — work with related records.
  • Model callbacks — attach behavior to a record's lifecycle.
  • Forms — accept input and redisplay validation errors.
  • Fields — choose column types and understand casting.

items.title: Model associations
items.text:
Associations connect related models. An author has many posts; a post belongs to an author. Declare those relationships once, then use them to find, build, and save related records.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Declare one-to-many and one-to-one relationships.
  • Build and query records through an association.
  • Model a many-to-many relationship with a join model.
  • Save related records from a nested form.

This guide builds on Model basics. Create the related tables through migrations before using their associations.

items.title: Association declarations
items.text:
Declare both sides of the relationship in their model classes:

# app/models/author.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_many, validates


class Author(ApplicationModel):
    has_many("posts", dependent="destroy")
    validates("name", presence=True)

# app/models/post.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import belongs_to, validates


class Post(ApplicationModel):
    belongs_to("author")
    validates("title", presence=True)

Generate Post with author:references to add its author_id foreign key. Names and keys are inferred by convention. Use class_name or foreign_key when the schema uses different names. Associations require single-column primary keys.

A belongs_to target is required by default. Use optional=True when a record can exist without it. For a single related record, use has_one("profile") instead of has_many("profiles"), with the foreign key on the profile table.

Assign the relationship rather than just its foreign key to keep both sides consistent:

author = Author.create(name="Ada")
post = Post.new(title="First", author=author)
post.save()

items.title: Work through a collection
items.text:
An association keeps queries scoped to its owner:

post = author.posts.create(title="Next")
posts = author.posts.where(title="Next").order(title="asc")
first_post = author.posts.first()
post_count = author.posts.count()

create() requires a saved parent and returns the child even if validation fails. Check its errors just as you would after Post.create(). To build a parent and child before saving either, use new():

author = Author.new(name="Grace")
author.posts.new(title="First")
author.save()

Saving the parent validates and saves its new children in the same transaction. By default, it does not save edits to existing children. Use autosave=True on an association when those edits should be saved with the parent.

items.title: Query saved records or read the current collection
items.text:
A collection can contain unsaved additions as well as saved records.

  • count() counts saved rows.
  • len(author.posts) loads the collection, including unsaved additions.
  • size() uses loaded contents when available; otherwise it counts saved rows plus pending new records.
  • first() and last() use loaded contents when available. An explicit query, such as author.posts.order(title="asc").first(), selects saved rows.

Filters and ordering return a new query; keep the result. They do not rearrange an already-loaded collection.

items.title: Refresh a collection
items.text:
Use author.posts.reload() to replace its visible contents with fresh saved records, without discarding the author's own pending fields or errors. Previously held child objects keep their input and remain saveable.

Use author.reload() instead when you want to abandon the owner's loaded input graph. Reloading does not save or delete records.

items.title: Many-to-many relationships through a join model
items.text:
Use a join model when the relationship has data of its own. An organization has users through memberships, and each membership records the user's role.

Generate the models and migrate their tables:

bin/flask generate model Organization name:string
bin/flask generate model User name:string
bin/flask generate model Membership organization:references user:references role:string
bin/flask db:migrate

Add these declarations to the generated classes, importing has_many, belongs_to, and validates from flaskteroids.model in the files that use them:

class Organization(ApplicationModel):
    has_many("memberships", dependent="destroy")
    has_many("users", through="memberships")


class Membership(ApplicationModel):
    belongs_to("organization")
    belongs_to("user")
    validates("role", presence=True)


class User(ApplicationModel):
    has_many("memberships", dependent="destroy")
    has_many("organizations", through="memberships")

Create the relationship with its role, then query the related users:

organization = Organization.create(name="Example")
user = User.create(name="Ada")
organization.memberships.create(user=user, role="administrator")
members = organization.users.where(name="Ada")

The source association is inferred from the collection name. For a different name, use has_many("members", through="memberships", source="user").

items.title: Build, add, and remove targets
items.text:
When collection operations do not need additional membership input, you can work directly with users:

organization.users.append(existing_user)
organization.users.remove(existing_user)

For the membership above, first give role a database default in a migration; otherwise the new membership fails its presence validation.

For a saved owner, through-collection creation, append, removal, clear, and replacement write immediately. They commit before returning or join an explicit transaction. Adding an existing target also saves its pending scalar edits.

A rejected append or replacement raises RecordInvalid from flaskteroids.model. Inspect error.record.errors to show the failing target or membership's errors. Let the exception escape a transaction block if the whole group should roll back.

Removing a user deletes memberships, not the user. It does not run membership destroy callbacks; explicitly destroy the membership when those callbacks are needed. Add a database unique constraint on the two foreign keys if the same membership must not appear twice.

Through collections cache their loaded targets. After changing a membership directly, call organization.users.reload() to see the updated membership. Reloading this collection leaves pending joins in organization.memberships; use organization.reload() to abandon the whole loaded input graph.

Through associations support a direct has_many join and a direct belongs_to source. Nested through paths and polymorphic sources are not supported.

items.title: Autosave and nested attributes
items.text:
Nested attributes let one form edit a parent and its children. Opt in on the parent model after declaring the association:

# app/models/order.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import accepts_nested_attributes_for, has_many


class Order(ApplicationModel):
    has_many("line_items", dependent="destroy")
    accepts_nested_attributes_for(
        "line_items", allow_destroy=True, reject_if="all_blank", limit=20
    )

This enables autosave for the association. Assign child input, then save the parent:

order.line_items_attributes = [
    {"id": existing_item.id, "quantity": "3"},
    {"description": "New item", "quantity": "1"},
    {"id": removed_item.id, "_destroy": "1"},
]
if not order.save():
    messages = order.errors["line_items[0].quantity"]

An id updates only a child in this association; unrelated or missing IDs raise RecordNotFoundException. Without an ID, input builds a new child. allow_destroy=True permits deletion of an existing child on save. reject_if="all_blank" ignores empty rows, and limit=20 bounds the number of submitted rows.

The parent and participating children validate and save together. Failed validation retains their original input and errors for redisplay. Nested attributes require a single primary key named id. For a through association, accept nested attributes on the join model (memberships), not the targets (users).

Continue with Nested forms to build the fields and permit their parameters.

items.title: Association changes and validation failures
items.text:
Association edits are not staged like scalar attributes. A failed validation does not undo an earlier append or removal. Remove an abandoned invalid new child from the collection instead of leaving it pending.

A standalone parent save commits the related records together. Inside an explicit transaction, a False result does not abort the block: raise an exception if the group must roll back. See Transactions.

items.title: Load associations together
items.text:
When listing posts and their authors, preload the authors to avoid a separate query for each post:

posts = Post.includes("author")
for post in posts:
    print(post.author.name)

Use dotted paths, such as Author.includes("posts.author"), for nested associations.

items.title: Deletion
items.text:
With dependent="destroy", destroying an author also destroys its posts in the same transaction, including their framework callbacks and attachment cleanup. A rejected standalone destruction returns False and rolls back the operation.

Native SQLAlchemy deletion and database cascades do not run framework child destroy callbacks. Database ON DELETE behavior is configured in migrations and is not a replacement for callback-aware destruction.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: Use Forms to edit related records, or Model callbacks to attach behavior to their lifecycle.

items.title: Model callbacks
items.text:
Callbacks run shared behavior at points in a record's lifecycle. For example, a product can notify subscribers after its stock changes, regardless of which controller saved it.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Declare a callback and choose when it runs.
  • Limit a callback with a condition.
  • Inspect saved changes and run side effects after commit.

This guide assumes you can create and save models. For callbacks around HTTP requests, see Controller callbacks.

items.title: Start with a save callback
items.text:
Declare the callback inside the model and define its method on the same class:

# app/models/author.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import before_save


class Author(ApplicationModel):
    before_save("_normalize_name")

    def _normalize_name(self):
        if self.name:
            self.name = self.name.strip()

Saving an author now normalizes its name before writing it. Keep callbacks for behavior that should accompany every save; call a regular method when the behavior belongs to just one application workflow.

items.title: Choose a callback
items.text:
Choose the lifecycle event that matches the behavior. Available events include:

  • Before/after validation.
  • Before/around/after save, create, update, and destroy.
  • After initialize/find.
  • After commit/rollback.

Before callbacks can return False to halt an operation. Around callbacks are generators that yield once. A callback can assign attributes before saving.

items.title: Conditional callbacks
items.text:
Use when to run a callback only when a condition is true. In the Author example, replace the callback declaration and add this condition method:

    before_save("_normalize_name", when="_needs_normalization")

    def _needs_normalization(self):
        return self.name is not None and self.name != self.name.strip()

Use unless instead when a true condition should skip the callback. A condition can be a method name or a callable receiving the record.

items.title: Callback timing
items.text:
After-find runs before after-initialize when a record is loaded from the database. These load callbacks do not rerun when a query returns an already-loaded object.

After-commit callbacks wait for the outer transaction to commit. They do not run when a nested savepoint is released. Native and bulk writes do not trigger framework save or commit callbacks.

items.title: Saved changes
items.text:
Use saved_change_to_attribute() to compare the old and new values after a successful save. It returns a pair of values, or None when the attribute did not change.

For example, notify subscribers when stock goes from zero to a positive number. This example assumes the product's inventory field, subscribers, and mailer from the Restock notifications tutorial:

from app.mailers.product_mailer import ProductMailer
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import after_commit


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    after_commit("_notify_subscribers", on="update", when="_back_in_stock")

    def _back_in_stock(self):
        change = self.saved_change_to_attribute("inventory_count")
        return change is not None and change[0] == 0 and change[1] > 0

    def _notify_subscribers(self):
        for subscriber in self.subscribers:
            ProductMailer.with_params(
                product=self, subscriber=subscriber
            ).in_stock().deliver_later()

Saved changes describe the latest successful save, not pending input or every change in a transaction. After repeated saves in one transaction, the commit callback sees the last successful save. Rollback and reload() clear saved changes; native and bulk writes do not produce them.

items.title: Choose the right callback for side effects
items.text:
Use after_commit for work that leaves the database, such as enqueueing email. At that point the worker can read the saved records. A failure in an after-commit callback cannot undo the completed commit.

New attachment uploads are also available after commit, not in after_save. See Attachments.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: Follow Restock notifications to build a complete callback-driven email feature, or read Background jobs to move work out of a request.

items.title: Attribute encryption
items.text:
Use attribute encryption to keep sensitive strings out of your database in plaintext. Your application still reads and assigns normal strings; Flaskteroids encrypts database writes and decrypts reads automatically.

This is different from encrypted credentials: credentials protect application secrets in a file, while attribute encryption protects model data in database columns. The two features use separate keys.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Set up dedicated encryption keys.
  • Encrypt model attributes and choose an appropriate query mode.
  • Migrate existing values and rotate randomized-encryption keys.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
From your application directory, generate keys and open the credentials editor:

bin/flask db:encryption:init
bin/flask credentials:edit

The first command only prints new keys. Copy its YAML into the editor:

encryption:
  primary_key: <generated primary key>
  deterministic_key: <generated deterministic key>
  • primary_key encrypts ordinary attributes and encrypted rich-text bodies.
  • deterministic_key encrypts attributes declared with deterministic=True, which support equality lookups.

Neither key is a database primary key. Neither the credentials master key nor Flask's signing secret is reused for attribute encryption.

Do not commit or log the printed keys. Store them in encrypted credentials or supply them through your deployment's secret management. Use separate keys for each application and environment, including tests. Keep keys separate from database backups, and retain the keys needed to restore older backups.

items.title: Other ways to supply keys
items.text:
You can use environment variables instead of credentials:

FLASKTEROIDS_ENCRYPTION_PRIMARY_KEY
FLASKTEROIDS_ENCRYPTION_DETERMINISTIC_KEY

Or set config.encryption.primary_key and config.encryption.deterministic_key in application configuration. The lookup order is explicit configuration → environment → credentials.

Keys are base64-encoded 32-byte values, not passwords. Python code can generate one with flaskteroids.encryption.generate_encryption_key().

items.title: Declare attributes
items.text:
Create ordinary string or text columns through migrations. Prefer text because encryption increases the stored size:

bin/flask generate model Customer name:string email:text notes:text
bin/flask db:migrate

Add the declarations to app/models/customer.py:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import encrypts, validates


class Customer(ApplicationModel):
    encrypts("notes")
    encrypts("email", deterministic=True, downcase=True)

    validates("name", presence=True)
    validates("email", presence=True)

Use the model normally:

customer = Customer.create(
    name="Ada",
    email="Ada@EXAMPLE.COM",
    notes="Private notes",
)
customer.email                          # "ada@example.com"
customer.notes                          # "Private notes"
customer.update(notes="Revised notes")
customer.reload().notes                 # "Revised notes"
Customer.encrypted_attributes()          # frozenset({"email", "notes"})
customer.ciphertext_for("notes")         # Ciphertext rather than plaintext

encrypts accepts several names with the same options, and declarations can be inherited from abstract model bases and concerns. downcase=True lowercases assignment and query input; it does not preserve original casing.

If the columns already contain plaintext, follow the migration steps below before serving traffic. Adding a declaration alone does not convert existing rows.

items.title: Storage requirements
items.text:
• Use real string/text columns. Primary keys and foreign keys cannot be encrypted.
  • Do not use plaintext database defaults on encrypted columns. Set defaults through application assignment or initialization callbacks instead.
  • Unique indexes and constraints require deterministic=True.
  • None stays SQL NULL; an empty string is encrypted.

A limited string column is allowed, but oversized ciphertext raises EncryptionError without exposing plaintext in the message. Prefer text and use model length validations for user-facing limits.

No companion ciphertext column or custom SQLAlchemy mapping is needed. Only one model class per application registry may map to an encrypted table.

items.title: Queries
items.text:
Choose the mode according to how you need to use the field:

Mode Same value written twice Supported lookups Randomized, the default Different ciphertexts NULL checks Deterministic Same ciphertext within the same attribute context Equality, inequality, IN, NOT IN, and NULL checks

Use randomized encryption unless you need equality lookups or a unique index. Deterministic encryption reveals which values are equal and how often they occur.

Customer.find_by(email="ADA@example.com")
Customer.where(email="ada@example.com")
Customer.where(Customer.email.in_(["ada@example.com", "grace@example.com"]))
Customer.where(notes=None)

Substring searches, range comparisons, and framework ordering raise EncryptionError. Ciphertext does not preserve plaintext sort order.

Mapped SQLAlchemy selects, inserts, and updates use the same encryption types. Raw SQL and explicit type coercion bypass them. Raw filters are not rewritten, and native ordering/grouping does not gain plaintext semantics. Do not use raw SQL writes for encrypted values.

items.title: Forms, validation, inspection, and fixtures
items.text:
Forms and validations work with plaintext. A failed validation keeps the submitted value for redisplay, and change tracking uses plaintext values.

Encrypted attributes are omitted from model repr. SQL parameters that pass through mapped encrypted types contain ciphertext. These protections do not cover logs of request bodies, form values, or model changes.

Rendered HTML and JSON serialization still contain plaintext. Authorize access to those responses. Use _serialization_exclude or explicit serializers to omit sensitive fields where needed; encryption does not make them safe to expose.

YAML fixtures use ordinary plaintext values. The fixture loader encrypts declared attributes automatically. Configure dedicated test keys; no encrypt_fixtures switch is needed.

items.title: Direct use outside models
items.text:
Use the same service for UTF-8 strings that are not model attributes:

from config.environment import application
from flaskteroids.encryption import decrypt, encrypt

with application.app_context():
    ciphertext = encrypt("Sensitive value", context="external_service.token")
    plaintext = decrypt(ciphertext, context="external_service.token")

Choose a stable, purpose-specific context. Decryption requires the same context. Both calls default to randomized encryption with the primary key. To use the deterministic key, pass deterministic=True to both calls. Requests and jobs already have an application context.

items.title: Rotate the primary key
items.text:
Configure randomized-encryption keys from oldest to newest:

config.encryption.primary_key = [previous_key, current_key]

The last key encrypts new writes; all listed keys may decrypt. Inside an application context, re-encrypt existing records before removing an old key:

for customer in Customer.all():
    customer.encrypt()

encrypt() requires a saved record. It updates encrypted attributes without saving unrelated pending attributes or running save callbacks and validations. It participates in model transactions. New records use normal saves.

items.title: Keep the deterministic key stable
items.text: The deterministic key must be a single key, not a list. Changing it breaks existing equality queries and unique-index behavior. Online rotation and queries across multiple encryption schemes are not supported. Plan a data/index migration instead of simply replacing this key.

items.title: Convert existing plaintext
items.text:
Plaintext in an encrypted column is rejected by default. To migrate it:

  1. Back up the data and stop normal traffic and workers.
  2. Temporarily allow plaintext reads:
config.encryption.support_unencrypted_data = True
  1. Load records and call record.encrypt() inside an application context.
  2. Verify the data, remove the setting, and only then resume traffic.

This setting permits plaintext reads; writes remain encrypted. Wrong keys, modified ciphertext, malformed envelopes, and unsupported envelope versions still raise EncryptionError.

items.title: Re-encrypt rich text
items.text:
Rich text uses the same primary keys, but has its own operation:

for post in Post.with_rich_text_content():
    post.content.encrypt()

This also converts existing plaintext bodies without enabling plaintext reads. See Rich text.

items.title: Security and limitations
items.text:
Randomized encryption uses AES-256-GCM with a fresh 96-bit nonce. Deterministic encryption uses the cryptography library's AES-256-SIV primitive with a domain-separated, HKDF-derived key.

Both modes authenticate the model/attribute context. Moving ciphertext to another attribute fails authentication. Renaming a model or encrypted attribute requires decrypting and re-encrypting its data under the new context, not just renaming the declaration. Stored values use Flaskteroids-specific versioned envelopes.

Encryption protects database contents, not a running application holding its keys. It can still reveal value lengths, NULLs, and deterministic equality. It does not protect process memory, application logs, rendered responses, uploaded file bytes, or attachment metadata. Use storage-provider encryption and download authorization for files. Use has_secure_password for passwords, not reversible encryption.

Custom key providers, encryption that ignores case while preserving original casing, non-string/serialized attributes, a model operation that writes decrypted plaintext, and online multi-scheme deterministic queries are not supported.

items.title: Assets
items.text:
Put stylesheets, images, and fonts in app/assets. They work without a build in development. For production, precompile them into files with content hashes in their names, so browsers can cache them safely.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Add stylesheets, images, and fonts to your application.
  • Reference them from templates and CSS.
  • Build and serve fingerprinted assets in production.

items.title: Add source assets
items.text:
Put stylesheets in app/assets/stylesheets, images in app/assets/images, and fonts in app/assets/fonts. JavaScript belongs in app/javascript; see Import maps to load modules.

Development serves source files directly at /assets/; no build command is needed. Keep these files public: assets are not private attachment storage.

items.title: Link assets from templates
items.text:
Generated layouts already link app/assets/stylesheets/application.css:

{{ stylesheet_link_tag("application", **{"data-turbo-track": "reload"}) }}
<img src="{{ asset_path("logo.png") }}" alt="Logo">

Helpers are also available from flaskteroids.helpers. stylesheet_link_tag appends .css, accepts multiple names and escaped HTML attributes, and returns trusted markup.

Names are relative to the source root, such as stylesheets/application.css. Short names search immediate subdirectories: application.css and logo.png resolve into stylesheets/ and images/. Ambiguous names raise AssetError; use directory-qualified names to disambiguate.

Helpers generate source URLs in development. In production, they read the build manifest to find the fingerprinted filename. A fingerprint is a content hash: when a file changes, its URL changes too.

Native url_for("static", filename=...) works, but does not look up fingerprints.

items.title: Local Turbo runtime
items.text: New browser applications load Turbo from the installed flaskteroids-turbo package. Do not add a second runtime. See Turbo setup to install or upgrade it.

items.title: CSS references
items.text:
Use ordinary file-relative paths. In stylesheets/application.css:

@import "themes/base.css";
.hero { background-image: url("../images/logo.png"); }
@font-face { font-family: Demo; src: url("../fonts/demo.woff2"); }

Precompilation includes all non-hidden asset subdirectories, including fonts/. It rewrites local CSS URLs and imports to point to fingerprinted files, keeping query strings and fragments. Changing an image or font also changes the fingerprint of stylesheets that reference it.

Missing references or circular CSS dependencies fail the build before replacing the previous manifest.

items.title: CSS support and limits
items.text: The URL rewriter supports standard quoted/unquoted url(...), quoted @import, and normal CSS escapes in UTF-8 files. Comments, ordinary strings, external/data/absolute URLs, and fragment-only references stay unchanged. It is not a full CSS parser: escaped function names and string-only image-set() references are unsupported; use url(...) for those references. There is no Sass/JavaScript compilation, bundling, or minification.

items.title: Production builds
items.text:
bin/flask assets:precompile
# From outside the application:
flask assets:precompile --root /path/to/app

Both commands build without starting the application, accessing the database, reading runtime keys, or running initializers. The command is registered as a Flask CLI plugin, so plain flask assets:precompile is bootless too.

Deploy public/assets including its .manifest.json file. Generated Docker builds already precompile assets and keep the output in the image; generated ignore files exclude local build artifacts from Git and Docker input.

Builds are deterministic. If the manifest, an entry, or a compiled file is missing or invalid, helpers raise AssetError; production does not fall back to source files.

items.title: Public files and caching
items.text:
Everything in the served asset directory should be public. The manifest is a filename lookup, not an access-control list. Builds leave old fingerprinted files in place, so old URLs remain usable. Hidden paths and symlinks are rejected; missing or unsafe requests return 404.

Generated production configuration sets Flask's SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT to one year; successful compiled responses with positive cache lifetimes are also immutable. Set the native option to None for conditional revalidation or 0 for immediate revalidation. Without this configuration, Flask defaults to revalidation. The option also affects other send_file() calls without an explicit cache lifetime.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
config.assets.source_path = "app/assets"
config.assets.output_path = "public/assets"
config.assets.prefix = "/assets"
config.assets.serve = True

Set these options in application configuration. Source and output paths are relative to the project root, must remain inside the project, and cannot overlap. source_path configures the main asset directory; the conventional JavaScript sources and framework assets are also included. Source directories must not overlap. The URL prefix must be an absolute path with no query string; trailing slashes are normalized.

Internally, these options configure Flask's static_folder and static_url_path before its static route is registered. Production uses app.send_static_file; development resolves the appropriate source directory and uses Flask file delivery.

For example, use source_path = "frontend", output_path = "static", and prefix = "/custom/assets" to change the directories and URL independently. The bootless compiler does not read Python configuration; pass matching paths:

bin/flask assets:precompile --source frontend --output static

Exclude custom output directories from Git/Docker input and regenerate them in the build. Helpers respect deployment script prefixes.

items.title: Serve through a reverse proxy
items.text: To let a reverse proxy deliver files, serve the output at the configured prefix and set config.assets.serve = False; URL generation remains available. Configure MIME and cache headers, block dotfiles (including the manifest) and symlinks, and never expose source/project directories.

items.title: Attachments
items.text:
Use attachments to give a model one file, such as an avatar, or a collection of files, such as documents. File bytes live in a configured storage service; the database keeps attachment records and metadata.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Add single or multiple file uploads to a model.
  • Accept uploads in a form and display download links.
  • Choose storage, protect private files, and remove uploads.

items.title: Set up
items.text:
To generate a resource with file uploads, run these commands inside your application:

bin/flask generate scaffold User name:string avatar:attachment documents:attachments
bin/flask attachments:install
bin/flask db:migrate

Model, resource, and scaffold generators accept name:attachment for one file and name:attachments for multiple files. Here, avatar and documents are attachment names, not database columns. The scaffold generates the model declarations, upload inputs, controller parameters, and file links.

bin/flask attachments:install creates an attachment migration and adds config/storage.yml if missing. bin/flask db:migrate applies the migrations.

items.title: Add attachments to a model
items.text:
To add attachments to an existing model without a generator, declare them with has_one_attached or has_many_attached. Run bin/flask attachments:install and bin/flask db:migrate if attachments have not been set up yet.

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_one_attached, has_many_attached


class User(ApplicationModel):
    has_one_attached("avatar")
    has_many_attached("documents")

Pass an uploaded file to attach, or include it in create or update:

user.avatar.attach(upload)
user.update(avatar=another_upload)
user.documents.attach(first_upload, second_upload)

For multiple files, attach adds to the collection; user.update(documents=[upload]) replaces it. For a new record or one with unsaved changes, call save() after attaching.

You can also attach an open file:

with open("avatar.png", "rb") as stream:
    user.avatar.attach(io=stream, filename="avatar.png")

Use user.avatar.attached() to check for a file and user.avatar.filename to read its name.

items.title: When files become available
items.text:
Uploads become available after commit:

  • A standalone save commits before returning.
  • Attaching to a saved record with no pending changes also commits before returning.
  • Inside Model.transaction(), uploads wait for the block to commit.
  • In model callbacks, read new uploads in after_commit, not after_save.

Standalone blob creation and explicit attachment removal also commit their own transaction unless they join an explicit block.

items.title: Upload forms
items.text:
{% call(form) form_with(model=user) %}
  {{ form.label("avatar") }}
  {{ form.file_field("avatar") }}

  {{ form.label("documents") }}
  {% for document in user.documents %}
    {{ form.hidden_field("documents", multiple=True, value=document.signed_id()) }}
  {% endfor %}
  {{ form.file_field("documents", multiple=True) }}
  {{ form.submit() }}
{% endcall %}

form_with handles multipart encoding. The hidden fields keep existing documents; without them, submitting the multiple file field replaces the collection, including clearing it when no files are selected. An empty single file input keeps the existing attachment.

Permit uploads in your controller:

attributes = self.params.expect(user=["avatar", ("documents", [])])
user.update(**attributes)

expect requires the outer user dictionary, not every permitted upload field. Keep a fixed allowlist: omitted fields are excluded from attributes, so a partial update leaves their attachments unchanged. To clear a collection, submit an empty list explicitly rather than omitting the field.

items.title: Validation and limits
items.text:
Replace the existing avatar declaration inside User with one that includes size and content-type checks. Keep its other declarations and methods:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_one_attached


class User(ApplicationModel):
    has_one_attached(
        "avatar",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )

    # Keep other declarations and methods here.

Failed checks add messages to the model's errors and prevent saving. Content-type checks do not replace file scanning.

There is no per-file size limit by default. Set limits in your configuration:

config.attachments.max_upload_size = 20 * 1024 * 1024  # Per file
config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"] = 25 * 1024 * 1024        # Entire request

Uploads over these limits return HTTP 413.

items.title: Download links
items.text:
Use blob_path in templates:

{% if user.avatar.attached() %}
  <img src="{{ blob_path(user.avatar) }}" alt="Avatar">
{% endif %}

blob_path returns a relative link; blob_url returns an absolute URL. Both are also available from flaskteroids.attachments in Python. Use blob_path(user.avatar, disposition="attachment") to force a download, or pass expires_in=3600 for a link that expires after an hour.

Application links are permanent by default. user.avatar.url() instead returns a direct storage URL that normally expires after five minutes.

Anyone holding a signed link can download the file by default. A signature prevents tampering; it does not check who is using the link. Share links and signed IDs only with authorized users, or add the permission check below.

items.title: Private files
items.text:
Define can_download(blob) in app/helpers/permissions.py to check permissions and return True or False. Configure it in an initializer:

# config/initializers/attachments.py
from flask import current_app
from app.helpers.permissions import can_download

current_app.config.attachments.authorize = can_download
current_app.config.attachments.resolve_model_to_route = "proxy"

The callback receives a blob (the stored file record). It can inspect blob.attachments to check ownership and the browser session to identify the user. Download routes do not run controller authentication callbacks. Denied downloads return 404.

Use blob_path or blob_url for private files. Direct storage URLs bypass the permission check, so avoid user.avatar.url() and public storage for those files.

items.title: Storage
items.text:
Edit config/storage.yml to define your services:

local:
  service: Disk
  root: storage

test:
  service: Disk
  root: tmp/storage

archive:
  service: Disk
  root: storage/archive

Relative disk paths start at the application root. Keep the storage directory persistent when deploying containers. Generated Docker applications use writable /app/storage for SQLite and local uploads; mount persistent storage there. Host bind mounts must be writable by the image user. bin/setup and default web startup create only conventional storage, not arbitrary configured directories.

Disk storage is built in. Additional providers are installed separately and register through the flaskteroids.storage entry point group. No application import or initializer is needed. Installation makes a provider available; it does not change the selected service. Follow the provider package's documentation for its configuration and credentials.

For example, flaskteroids-storage-s3 provides S3-compatible storage; its setup and provider-specific options are documented in that package.

Select a service in your environment configuration:

config.attachments.service = "archive"

Generated applications use local in development and test in tests. Production uses FLASKTEROIDS_ATTACHMENTS_SERVICE, defaulting to local. A declaration can override the default with service="archive". Changing services does not move existing files.

items.title: Custom storage providers
items.text: Additional storage services are supplied by provider packages. Installing a provider makes it available; select it in config/storage.yml and follow the package's setup instructions. A missing or invalid selected provider fails explicitly rather than falling back to local storage.

items.title: Remove files
items.text:
user.avatar.detach()       # Keep the file, remove the attachment
user.avatar.purge_later()  # Delete the file in a background job
user.avatar.purge()        # Delete the file now

Replacing attachments or deleting their record schedules file deletion by default. Run your Celery worker to process these jobs. Shared files are not purged while another attachment uses them.

Prefer purge_later in transactions and callbacks. Rolling back after purge does not restore the deleted file.

items.title: Unattached uploads
items.text:
A blob is a stored file record; it can exist without an attachment, for example after someone abandons an upload form. Cleanup is not scheduled automatically.

Schedule a job that calls Blob.purge_unattached() to enqueue deletion of unattached blobs older than two days. Use a positive older_than=timedelta(...) to choose another grace period. This covers all unattached blobs, including rich-text uploads. Purge jobs recheck attachments before deleting files.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
Place files in test/fixtures/files and attach them in your tests:

from test.test_helper import fixture_file_upload

user.avatar.attach(fixture_file_upload("avatar.png"))

Tests use temporary local storage, even when the application uses a remote provider. Browser tests can use self.attach_file("Avatar", "test/fixtures/files/avatar.png"). See Testing for test setup.

items.title: Using the command line
items.text:
Run commands from your application directory with bin/flask; no environment activation is needed. You can also use flask in an activated environment or uv run flask.

Use bin/flask --help to list commands, or add --help to a specific command:

bin/flask generate --help
bin/flask db:migrate --help

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Create an application and generate its components.
  • Prepare the database and work in the application shell.
  • Find commands for testing and other framework features.

items.title: Generation and setup
items.text:
flask new my_app
cd my_app
bin/flask run

A new app has its dependencies installed and development database prepared. For a fresh checkout, run bin/setup first.

To generate files without installing, use flask new my_app --skip-install and run bin/setup later. Commit uv.lock so the team shares dependency versions.

For an API instead of server-rendered pages, pass --api when creating the application. Controller and scaffold generators then produce API output. See Building an API for a complete example.

items.title: Database preparation
items.text:
Migrations describe changes to database tables. To create a database if necessary and apply pending migrations:

bin/flask db:prepare

Select another environment with FLASKTEROIDS_ENV:

FLASKTEROIDS_ENV=test bin/flask db:prepare
FLASKTEROIDS_ENV=production bin/flask db:prepare

Preparation does not reset the database or seed records.

Command When to use it db:prepare Create a database if needed and bring it up to date db:create Create a database without applying migrations db:migrate Apply pending migrations to an existing database db:rollback Undo the most recent migration db:init Add migration setup to an app that does not have it db:schema:dump Refresh db/schema.py without changing database data

New applications already include migration setup.

items.title: After a migration
items.text:
Successful migrations regenerate db/schema.py from the selected database. Commit this generated snapshot, but do not edit its columns by hand. Restart servers and workers afterward so they load the new schema.

Review migrations and rollbacks before running them in production: either can delete data. If a command fails, fix the reported problem and retry; the database is left available for inspection. If migrations succeed but writing the snapshot fails, fix the file/access problem and run bin/flask db:schema:dump. A failed snapshot write does not undo database changes.

items.title: Startup and connection requirements
items.text:
Database commands use normal application startup, including initializers. New models can be imported before their tables appear in the snapshot, but an initializer that constructs or queries an unavailable model still fails. There is no separate migration-only startup mode.

For PostgreSQL or MySQL, start the server and configure the connection first. For SQLite, use a file rather than :memory: and ensure its parent directory exists.

items.title: Shell
items.text:
Open an application-aware Python shell:

bin/flask shell

Your models and session are available:

user = User.create(name="Alice")  # Commits before returning.
with User.transaction():
    user.update(name="Alicia")
    User.create(name="Bob")
# Both changes commit at the end of the block.

Standalone save(), create(), update(), and destroy() commit immediately. Inside Model.transaction(), they join the block's transaction. An exception escaping the block rolls the group back; a False save result does not.

Shell exit rolls back unfinished work, not earlier standalone commits. Native SQLAlchemy writes need explicit commit/transaction handling. To discard pending model input, use record.discard_changes() or record.reload(). See model transactions.

items.title: Credentials
items.text:
bin/flask credentials:edit
bin/flask credentials:show
bin/flask credentials:edit --environment production

edit opens encrypted YAML for editing. show prints decrypted secrets: do not copy its output into logs. Environment-specific credentials replace shared ones; they do not merge with them. See encrypted credentials for key setup.

items.title: Generators
items.text: Use bin/flask generate to create application components. Fields use name:type, such as title:string. See Fields for supported types and modifiers. The examples below use concrete names; replace them with your application's names.

items.title: Migration
items.text: Generate a migration, review it, then apply it with bin/flask db:migrate. Generating the file alone does not change the database or schema snapshot.

items.title: Create a table
items.text:
bin/flask generate migration CreateProducts name:string!

Use the plural table name after Create, without a Table suffix. New tables include an auto-incrementing id, created_at, and updated_at.

items.title: Add columns
items.text: bin/flask generate migration AddPriceToProducts price:float

items.title: Remove columns
items.text: bin/flask generate migration RemovePriceFromProducts price

items.title: Drop a table
items.text: bin/flask generate migration DropProducts

items.title: Model
items.text:
bin/flask generate model Post title:string author:references

Creates a model class, migration, and tests. References add belongs_to(...) declarations. Columns become available in the schema snapshot after migration.

items.title: Controller
items.text:
bin/flask generate controller Users index show

Creates a controller with the named actions, a view for each, and individual routes. It also creates app/helpers/users_helper.py with a UsersHelper class. Its public methods are available in templates without controller registration. See application helpers.

items.title: Resource
items.text:
bin/flask generate resource Product name:string price:float

Creates a model, migration, empty controller, and resource route. You write the controller actions and views.

items.title: Scaffold
items.text:
bin/flask generate scaffold Product name:string price:float

Creates a model, migration, resource route, controller, and views for the standard index, show, new, edit, create, update, and destroy actions. Apply the migration and restart the server before visiting the resource.

New controller/scaffold page templates use {% extends layout %} for frame-aware layout selection. Scaffold records use underscored dom_id values, and successful updates redirect with 303. Scaffolds remain ordinary full-page CRUD, not inline editors; see Turbo Frames and Streams to add that behavior.

items.title: Mailer
items.text:
bin/flask generate mailer User welcome_email

Creates UserMailer, text and HTML templates, a test, and preview scenarios in test/mailers/previews/user_mailer_preview.py. Supply the base name User, not UserMailer. Browse examples at /flaskteroids/mailers in development. See Preview emails for the walkthrough and Mailers for delivery configuration.

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
bin/flask generate authentication
bin/flask db:migrate

Creates a login and password-management workflow:

  • User with email_address and password_digest.
  • Session with user_id, ip_address, and user_agent.
  • Controllers and views for login and password changes.
  • Password-reset views and mailers.
  • Routes for session and password management.
  • An Authentication concern added to ApplicationController, requiring login by default and exposing the is_authenticated() template helper.

Create an account in the shell; no public sign-up form is generated. To allow a public action, declare skip_before_action("_require_authentication", only=[...]) inside its controller class. Templates can call is_authenticated() on public and protected pages without an extra callback. See the authentication walkthrough.

items.title: Work with other components
items.text:
Each component guide introduces its setup commands as part of a working example:

  • Attribute encryption — generate keys and encrypt attributes.
  • Turbo — install or upgrade the browser runtime.
  • Import maps — pin and maintain JavaScript packages.
  • Rich text — install the editor and its storage tables.
  • Attachments — install file storage.
  • Assets — precompile production files.
  • Middleware — inspect the request stack.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
bin/flask test
bin/flask test:system
bin/flask test test/models/post_test.py

test runs model, integration, job, and mailer tests. test:system runs browser tests. Both accept pytest arguments. See Testing for fixtures, assertions, and browser installation.

items.title: Commands outside an application
items.text:
flask new, flask agent-skills, flask assets:precompile, and flask importmap can run without loading an application. Install Flaskteroids in the Python environment that provides flask.

Outside an application, use a specific command's --help, such as flask new --help. Top-level flask --help attempts application discovery. Other application commands use normal startup, including initializers.

items.title: Fields
items.text:
Use name:type arguments when generating a migration, model, resource, or scaffold. For example, title:string creates a string column named title.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Choose field types when generating models and migrations.
  • Add required columns and references.
  • Understand how submitted values are cast and validated.

items.title: Column types
items.text:
Type Generator argument Text text String (255 characters) string or str Integer integer or int Float float Boolean boolean or bool Date and time datetime Date date Time time JSON json 
bin/flask generate model Post title:string! content:text published:boolean
bin/flask db:prepare

items.title: Required columns and references
items.text:
! makes a database column non-nullable, so it cannot store SQL NULL.

author:references (or author:belongs_to) adds a required foreign key and a belongs_to(...) declaration inside the generated model class. Database constraints do not replace user-facing validation; add validates(...) inside the model class when invalid input should return errors rather than a native constraint exception.

Change column definitions through migrations, not by editing the generated db/schema.py. The snapshot supplies model column types using SQLAlchemy's type system; there is no separate generator casting API.

items.title: Model casting and raw input
items.text:
When you assign a model attribute, Flaskteroids converts the value to its column type. This is casting, not validation: a value may convert successfully and still be invalid for your application. Changes stay pending until saved.

Read the converted value normally, or inspect the original input with read_attribute_before_type_cast(name).

  • String/text values stringify ordinary input; None remains None.
  • Integers accept numeric strings and numeric prefixes ("12extra" reads as 12). Blank input reads as None; nonnumeric strings read as zero but serialize as null. Add numericality validation to reject malformed original input.
  • Float/decimal values cast numeric strings; blank input reads as None.
  • Booleans cast "" to None. False values include False, 0, "0", "f", "F", "false", "FALSE", "off", and "OFF"; other non-null values are true.
  • Dates/times accept ISO-formatted strings and corresponding Python values. Invalid date/time strings read as None; the original input is retained for validation and form redisplay.
  • JSON values retain their Python structure and native SQLAlchemy serialization. Supported backend-specific types use SQLAlchemy's native database handling.
# For a Post model with an integer word_count column:
post = Post.new(word_count="12extra")
assert post.word_count == 12
assert post.read_attribute_before_type_cast("word_count") == "12extra"
# Add validates("word_count", numericality={"only_integer": True}) to reject it.

items.title: Nulls and defaults
items.text:
Omitting a value lets a database default apply. Explicitly assigning None stores null for ordinary scalar columns, even when a default exists.

Simple literal database defaults are available on new models without a query. Database functions and computed values populate on flush. Put persistent defaults in migrations; Python default functions cannot be recovered from a snapshot.

JSON's default serialization stores explicit None as JSON null, which reads back as None. JSON null is distinct from SQL NULL; an SQL IS NULL predicate does not necessarily match it. Primary-key generation remains native.

items.title: Rich text
items.text: Model, resource, and scaffold generators accept content:rich_text. This generates has_rich_text("content"), not a column on the owner. Scaffolds include a Lexxy editor, safe rendering, and permitted parameters. Run bin/flask rich_text:install, then bin/flask db:migrate. See Rich text.

items.title: Attachments
items.text: Model, resource, and scaffold generators accept avatar:attachment for a single file and documents:attachments for multiple files. These declare attachments, not scalar columns. Run bin/flask attachments:install, then apply the migrations with bin/flask db:migrate. See Attachments.

items.title: Forms
items.text:
A form has two parts: the template that builds inputs, and the controller that accepts their values. Use form_with to build the form and self.params.expect to choose which submitted attributes may reach your model.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Build a model-backed form and choose its fields.
  • Permit submitted attributes and redisplay invalid input.
  • Edit associated records with nested forms.

items.title: Building forms
items.text:
Pass a model to form_with. It chooses the destination and HTTP method, supplies field values, and includes a CSRF token. Inside the block, use form to create labels and inputs:

<!-- app/views/posts/_form.html -->
{% call(form) form_with(model=post) %}
  <div>
    {{ form.label("title") }}
    {{ form.text_field("title") }}
  </div>

  <div>
    {{ form.label("content") }}
    {{ form.text_area("content") }}
  </div>

  <div>
    {{ form.submit("Save") }}
  </div>
{% endcall %}

items.title: Destinations and HTTP methods
items.text:
For a conventional Post resource:

Model state Destination Method New record /posts POST Saved record /posts/<id> PATCH

Browsers submit PATCH as POST with a hidden _method field. Set method to override the default; method="PUT" also works for updates.

An explicit URL changes only the destination. The model still supplies values, errors, and default method inference:

{% call(form) form_with(model=post, url="/review", method="POST") %}
  {{ form.text_field("title") }}
  {{ form.submit("Review") }}
{% endcall %}

With a persisted post, omitting method="POST" here would infer PATCH, not POST. Ordinary nested model destinations accept a list or tuple:

{% call(form) form_with(model=[product, subscriber]) %}
  {{ form.email_field("email") }}
  {{ form.submit("Subscribe") }}
{% endcall %}

A new child submits to product_subscribers_path(product) with POST; a persisted child submits to product_subscriber_path(product, subscriber) with PATCH. Fields use the child prefix (subscriber[email]) and child values, including rejected input. scope="signup" overrides that prefix without changing the model that supplies values and errors. A missing parent identifier raises an error. Nested URLs do not automatically save nested model attributes.

items.title: Turbo and HTML attributes
items.text:
Pass HTML attributes directly to form_with, including nested data and aria dictionaries. class_ emits class; nested keys become dashed attributes:

{% call(form) form_with(model=post, class_="editor", data={"turbo_frame": dom_id(post)}) %}
  {{ form.text_field("title") }}
  {{ form.submit("Save") }}
{% endcall %}

Use data={"turbo_frame": "_top"} to navigate outside a frame, data={"turbo": False} to submit without Turbo, or data={"turbo_stream": True} to request Streams on a GET form. For Turbo validation failures, render HTML with 422; redirect successful mutations with 303 See Other. See the inline edit example and HTTP Streams.

items.title: Choose a field helper
items.text:
Field helpers include text_field, text_area, password_field, and checkbox. Use file_field('avatar') or file_field('documents', multiple=True) for uploads. form_with detects these fields and adds multipart encoding. See Attachments for attachment forms and permitted parameters.

Use form.rich_text_area("content") for declared rich-text attributes. Install Lexxy and storage with bin/flask rich_text:install, then migrate. See Rich text for setup, rendering, and validation.

items.title: Strong parameters
items.text:
Strong parameters are an allowlist of attributes a controller may pass to a model. Use self.params.expect for this filtering. Do not pass unfiltered request data to create or update: users could change fields you did not intend to expose, such as an admin flag.

expect also checks the input's structure, including nested objects and lists. For a post form:

# app/controllers/posts_controller.py
from app.models.post import Post
from flaskteroids.controller import Controller
from flaskteroids.routes import post_path


class PostsController(Controller):
    # ...

    def create(self):
        self.post = Post.new(**self._post_params())
        if self.post.save():
            return self.redirect_to(post_path(self.post), status=303)
        return self.render("new", status=422)

    def update(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])
        if self.post.update(**self._post_params()):
            return self.redirect_to(post_path(self.post), status=303)
        return self.render("edit", status=422)

    def _post_params(self):
        # Assumes form data is sent as:
        # post[title]=...
        # post[content]=...
        return self.params.expect(post=["title", "content"])

self.params.expect(post=["title", "content"]) requires a top-level post dictionary, but its nested fields are permitted, not required. It returns only submitted, permitted attributes and discards other attributes. The same allowlist works for both creation and partial updates:

# Submitted: post[content]=Updated
attributes = self.params.expect(post=["title", "content"])
# attributes == {"content": "Updated"}
post.update(**attributes)  # The existing title is unchanged.

This also applies recursively to nested dictionaries and arrays of dictionaries. Omitted fields are not filled with defaults; an explicitly submitted None scalar is retained. Use model validations to require attributes, rather than treating the allowlist as validation.

items.title: JSON-valued fields
items.text:
Use the explicit JSONValue schema marker for a field that accepts an entire JSON value, such as a JSON database column:

from flaskteroids.actions import JSONValue

attributes = self.params.expect(post=["title", ("settings", JSONValue)])

This permits objects with arbitrary string keys, arrays, strings, finite numbers, booleans, and null, including nested values and empty containers. The permission is limited to settings: other attributes still need their own allowlist entries. Uploads and arbitrary Python objects are rejected. Prefer an explicit nested schema when the permitted keys are known; JSONValue deliberately permits all JSON content inside that one field.

Scaffold generators use this schema automatically for name:json columns. Omitting the field leaves it unchanged during partial updates. JSON strings are values, not an invitation to decode another JSON document inside them.

items.title: Missing or malformed input
items.text:
• A missing, null, or empty root raises MissingParameter. This includes a dictionary with no permitted attributes left after filtering.
  • A required scalar root such as self.params.expect("password") rejects blank strings, but accepts False and numeric zero.
  • An incorrect type raises InvalidParameter. Optional fields must still have the expected structure when submitted.

During HTTP requests, Flaskteroids automatically translates MissingParameter and InvalidParameter into 400 Bad Request responses; controllers do not need to catch them. Browser controllers return an HTML error page, including when JSON is requested; API controllers return JSON errors. Applications can customize either response with Flask's register_error_handler() in an initializer (for example, to return JSON). Direct calls outside request dispatch still raise these exceptions. Programmer errors and unrelated exceptions are not translated into 400 responses.

items.title: Redisplay validation errors
items.text:
When saving fails, render the form with the submitted model and status 422. Do not redirect or load a fresh copy: the submitted object holds the values and errors the user needs to correct.

Add error messages to the form partial before its fields:

{% for message in post.errors.full_messages() %}
  <p role="alert">{{ message }}</p>
{% endfor %}

Fields show the original input, even when type conversion failed. Passwords must be entered again after a failed submission.

items.title: CSRF protection
items.text:
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is an attempt to make someone's browser submit an unwanted request while they are logged in. A session-bound token helps the server verify that a form came from your application.

Flaskteroids checks CSRF tokens on state-changing requests, meaning all methods except GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE. form_with and button_to include the token for unsafe forms, never GET forms. An overridden DELETE receives the same protection as an actual DELETE request. See Routing.

Tokens belong to the browser session and expire after one hour. Clearing the session invalidates its tokens; reload forms to obtain a new token. AJAX requests can send the token in the X-CSRF-TOKEN header instead of the csrf_token form field. Generated layouts also include <meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrf_token() }}"> for Turbo's request header. Add it to custom layouts when installing Turbo. Do not store pages containing CSRF tokens in a shared cache.

Include the token yourself in manual forms:

<form action="/posts" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{ csrf_token() }}">
  <!-- ... form fields -->
</form>

items.title: Buttons that submit forms
items.text:
{{ button_to("Create", "/products") }}
{{ button_to("Save", product) }}
{{ button_to("Delete", product, method="DELETE") }}
{{ button_to("Log out", session_path(), method="DELETE") }}

The default is POST for an explicit URL or new record and PATCH for a persisted record. Nested model sequences infer from the final record, just like forms. Deletion is always explicit. GET and POST render native HTML methods; PUT/PATCH/DELETE render POST plus the corresponding hidden override. GET forms include neither CSRF tokens nor method overrides, preventing tokens in query strings. Unsafe forms include a CSRF token.

Button attributes and form attributes are separate:

{{ button_to("Save", product, id="save-button", form={"id": "save-form", "class": "inline"}) }}

Labels and attributes are escaped; trusted Markup is permitted for labels, not unescaped attributes. Unsupported/executable destination schemes are rejected. Put Turbo data on the form with, for example, button_to("Delete", post, method="DELETE", form={"data": {"turbo_frame": "_top"}}).

items.title: Nested forms
items.text:
Declare accepts_nested_attributes_for() on the parent model, then use fields_for inside form_with. It calls the block once per associated child:

{% call(form) form_with(model=order) %}
  {{ form.label("number") }}
  {{ form.text_field("number") }}
  {% call(item) form.fields_for("line_items") %}
    <fieldset>
      {{ item.label("description") }}
      {{ item.text_field("description") }}
      {{ item.label("quantity") }}
      {{ item.number_field("quantity") }}
      {{ item.label("_destroy") }}
      {{ item.checkbox("_destroy") }}
      {% for message in item.errors.full_messages() %}
        <p role="alert">{{ message }}</p>
      {% endfor %}
    </fieldset>
  {% endcall %}
  {{ form.submit("Save order") }}
{% endcall %}

Fields use names such as order[line_items_attributes][0][quantity], with matching unique label/input IDs. Singular associations omit the collection index. Saved children receive a hidden id; use include_id=False only when you supply the identity yourself. item.model exposes the child and item.errors its validation errors. Raw rejected values and destruction checkboxes survive redisplay. Nested file fields make the outer form multipart, including at deeper nesting levels.

An empty association renders no fields. Build an initial row in the new or edit action when appropriate:

self.order.line_items.new()

Permit the nested fields explicitly; the declaration does not grant permission:

attributes = self.params.expect(
    order=[
        "number",
        ("line_items_attributes", [["id", "description", "quantity", "_destroy"]]),
    ]
)
if self.order.update(**attributes):
    return self.redirect_to(self.order, status=303)
return self.render("edit", status=422)

For a singular association, use a single field list, for example ("profile_attributes", ["id", "name", "_destroy"]). Re-render the submitted object on failure instead of replacing it with a fresh query or appending an extra blank row. See nested attributes for autosave, rejection, deletion, and transaction behavior. Dynamic add/remove JavaScript and automatic nested scaffold generation are not included.

items.title: Form values and escaping
items.text:
Forms show the original submitted scalar input before type conversion, plus assigned writable virtual fields. If there is no pending input, they use saved values. A failed validation therefore redisplays what the user entered, even if type conversion would otherwise lose information.

Authentication secrets, digests, confirmations, and reset tokens are excluded by default. Forms do not use JSON response serialization or evaluate read-only virtual fields such as reset tokens. Re-enter passwords after an unsuccessful submission.

Field names, prefixes, attribute values, input values, and textarea values are escaped. Keep field names and attribute names application-defined. Invalid HTML attribute names raise ValueError. Do not construct field attributes from unfiltered request data.

collection_select() escapes ordinary option labels and prompts. Explicit markupsafe.Markup is accepted for trusted labels and prompts, but option values and other field values are always escaped, even when supplied as Markup.

Form actions accept relative URLs, including protocol-relative URLs, and HTTP(S) URLs. Other schemes and URLs containing control characters raise ValueError. This policy prevents executable schemes; it does not restrict which hosts a form may submit to. Check destinations separately if they come from user input.

items.title: JavaScript with import maps
items.text:
Write browser-native JavaScript modules without Node, npm installation, bundling, or transpilation. Flaskteroids follows Rails' import-map workflow: declare logical module names, import them from JavaScript, and let the asset pipeline supply development or fingerprinted production URLs.

Browser applications include this setup. bin/flask importmap:install restores missing conventions without replacing application code. It adds the module helper to layouts without script tags; customized script layouts are left unchanged with setup instructions. Keep only one Turbo runtime.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Load application JavaScript and local modules.
  • Pin a third-party package without a JavaScript build step.
  • Deploy modules using fingerprinted asset URLs.

items.title: Application entrypoint
items.text:
app/javascript/application.js starts with:

import "@hotwired/turbo"

The generated layout loads it using:

{{ javascript_importmap_tags() }}

This emits the inline import map, configured module preloads, and a module script that imports application. The map precedes all module scripts. It is marked data-turbo-track="reload", so Turbo performs a full reload when a subsequent page has a changed map.

items.title: Pins and local modules
items.text:
Configuration is trusted Python with an explicit registration callback:

# config/importmap.py
def register(importmap):
    importmap.pin("application")
    importmap.pin("@hotwired/turbo", to="turbo.js")
    importmap.pin_all_from("app/javascript/lib", under="lib")

Then create app/javascript/lib/greeting.js:

export function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}`
}

And import it in application.js:

import { greet } from "lib/greeting"

document.addEventListener("turbo:load", () => {
  console.log(greet("Flaskteroids"))
})

A pin defaults to NAME.js; to= selects a different logical asset path. pin_all_from recursively registers .js and .mjs files. A directory's index.js is imported by the directory name: lib/index.js becomes lib. An optional to= prefix separates asset paths from the logical namespace.

Use pinned logical imports, not file-relative imports. For example, use "lib/greeting", not "./lib/greeting.js". The compiler does not rewrite JavaScript, so relative filenames will not follow production fingerprints.

Development/test rendering re-evaluates configuration and discovers added or removed local modules. Refresh the page to use changes; this is not hot module replacement. Production loads configuration at boot and caches resolved maps; restart application processes when deploying.

items.title: Third-party packages
items.text:
bin/importmap pin @github/hotkey
bin/importmap pin @github/hotkey@3.1.1
bin/importmap pin @github/hotkey --no-preload

The command calls JSPM's resolution API with browser/module conditions, downloads the returned dependencies to vendor/javascript, and writes pins into config/importmap.py. Package versions are recorded in pin comments and download provenance. Commit the configuration and downloaded files.

import { install } from "@github/hotkey"

Package maintenance commands:

bin/importmap packages          # List downloaded pins and recorded versions
bin/importmap update            # Resolve current versions of downloaded pins
bin/importmap pristine          # Redownload recorded versions
bin/importmap unpin @github/hotkey
bin/importmap json              # Inspect the resolved browser import map

unpin removes only explicitly named pins and their managed files. It preserves files referenced by other literal pins and does not automatically prune transitive dependencies. Remove unused dependency pins explicitly.

pin, update, and pristine accept --from jspm|unpkg|jsdelivr; resolution still uses JSPM's API. pin --env development requests development package builds. No service call is made during application startup or page rendering.

Commands run without application boot, credentials, or database access. From outside the application, use:

flask importmap --root /path/to/app pin @github/hotkey

Package commands preserve unrelated configuration. If pins are computed by custom Python rather than declared as literal importmap.pin(...) calls, edit them manually.

items.title: Packaged Turbo
items.text:
flaskteroids-turbo supplies the pinned Turbo 8.0.23 ESM build. Applications reference it through the @hotwired/turbo pin, rather than copying or downloading it. Upgrade the locked flaskteroids-turbo dependency to update the runtime.

An application can deliberately override turbo.js in app/javascript or vendor/javascript. Application assets take precedence over the packaged asset. Keep an override compatible with the framework's Turbo integration.

bin/flask turbo:install configures this same import-map workflow; it does not overwrite or refresh application-owned runtime files.

items.title: Preloads, additional entrypoints, and lazy imports
items.text:
Pins preload by default, avoiding serial discovery of deeply nested imports. Disable preloading for an optional module:

def register(importmap):
    importmap.pin("application")
    importmap.pin("editor", preload=False)
    importmap.pin("admin_support", preload="admin")
    importmap.pin("shared_support", preload=["application", "admin"])
    importmap.pin("admin")
