const editor = await import("editor")

Use {{ javascript_importmap_tags("admin") }} instead of the default helper for an alternate entrypoint. To load an additional pinned module on one page, put {{ javascript_import_module_tag("editor") }} after the main import-map helper. javascript_inline_importmap_tag and javascript_module_preload_tag are also available for advanced layouts. Do not emit duplicate maps.

items.title: Security, integrity, and caching
items.text:
All helpers are available from flaskteroids.helpers and in Jinja. Inline JSON and module names are escaped for script-element safety. Helpers accept nonce= for applications managing a Content Security Policy:

{{ javascript_importmap_tags(nonce=csp_nonce) }}

Enable optional integrity metadata:

def register(importmap):
    importmap.enable_integrity()
    importmap.pin("application")
    importmap.pin("optional", integrity=False)
    importmap.pin(
        "external",
        to="https://example.com/library-1.0.js",
        integrity="sha384-REPLACE_WITH_REAL_BASE64_HASH",
    )

Local SHA-384 hashes cover the actual served bytes, including production assets. Hashes appear in the map's integrity field and applicable preload links. External hashes are application-supplied. Browser support for import-map integrity varies; do not assume it universally enforces integrity on lazy-loaded modules.

If manually managing HTML ETags, include importmap_digest() in the validator alongside the page's own cache key. Otherwise an unchanged page validator could hide changed JavaScript mappings. This helper does not create validators or invoke conditional handling automatically.

items.title: Deploy JavaScript
items.text:
bin/flask assets:precompile
bin/importmap json --environment production

Precompilation includes application JavaScript, downloaded modules, and the flaskteroids-turbo runtime. It is deterministic, offline, and does not boot the app. Deploy the output with its manifest; the rendered map resolves logical names to fingerprinted URLs. Changing a dependency updates its mapping without rewriting the importing JavaScript. See Assets for custom paths and serving.

json accepts --source, --output, and --prefix when inspecting customized asset configurations; it does not load application settings automatically.

items.title: Choose compatible packages
items.text: Import maps support modern browsers' native ES modules. They do not compile TypeScript/JSX, convert arbitrary CommonJS packages, supply Node APIs, rewrite relative imports or import.meta.url assets, manage worker imports, or bundle JavaScript/CSS. Some packages require additional chunks or remote assets even after their entrypoints are downloaded. Verify a package's browser compatibility and complete asset graph rather than assuming arbitrary npm packages work offline. No legacy-browser shim is installed by default.

items.title: Internationalization
items.text:
Keep application text in YAML catalogs and select a locale around each request or operation. Flaskteroids provides Rails-style translation keys and helpers without additional dependencies. This translates application messages, not database content.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Translate application text with YAML catalogs.
  • Choose a locale for each request.
  • Translate plural messages and format dates and times.

items.title: Configure locales
items.text:
New applications include config/locales/en.yml:

en:
  hello: "Hello world"

Enable the locales your application supports in config/application.py:

config.i18n.default_locale = "en"
config.i18n.available_locales = ["en", "es"]

The default locale must be available. Locale identifiers are application-defined, case-sensitive strings, such as en, es, or pt-BR; there is no bundled language database. Merely adding a catalog does not enable a locale.

Catalogs are UTF-8 .yml or .yaml files under config/locales, including nested directories. Each file starts with one or more locale mappings. The filename does not select the locale:

# config/locales/products.yml
en:
  products:
    index:
      title: "Products"
    create:
      notice: "Product created"
es:
  products:
    index:
      title: "Productos"
    create:
      notice: "Producto creado"

Use nested string keys rather than dots in YAML keys. Quote keys such as "on", "off", "yes", and "no", which YAML otherwise interprets as booleans. Files merge in sorted path order, so prefer unique keys across catalogs.

Restart the application after editing catalogs or locale configuration.

items.title: Translate text
items.text:
In Python:

from flaskteroids.i18n import t, with_locale

with with_locale("es"):
    title = t("products.index.title")  # Productos

english = t("products.index.title", locale="en")

t is an alias for translate. Both require an application context. An explicit locale= applies only to that call. get_locale() returns the current selection, or the configured default.

In Jinja:

<h1>{{ t("products.index.title") }}</h1>

In app/views/products/index.html, a relative key uses the template context:

<h1>{{ t(".title") }}</h1>

An included products/_row.html uses products.row as its relative scope. Jinja inheritance and imported macros can share the caller's context; use fully qualified keys in shared layouts and macros rather than relying on their filenames for relative lookup. Imported macros need with context to receive request and application helpers.

Controllers also expose self.t / self.translate. Relative keys use the current controller and action:

# Inside ProductsController.create:
self.redirect_to(self.products_path(), notice=self.t(".notice"))

Other Python code uses absolute keys or an explicit string scope:

t("index.title", scope="products")

items.title: Interpolation
items.text:
Keep the whole message in the catalog so translators can reorder its parts:

en:
  greeting: "Hello %{name}!"
es:
  greeting: "¡Hola %{name}!"

{{ t("greeting", name=user.name) }}

Missing interpolation arguments raise MissingInterpolationArgument. Replacement values are not interpreted again as translation placeholders. locale, scope, default, and count are helper options; count is also available for interpolation.

items.title: Missing translations and fallbacks
items.text:
By default, a missing key produces diagnostic text, such as translation missing: es.products.index.title. Supply a literal default when appropriate:

t("navigation.help", default="Help")

To raise MissingTranslation instead, enable this setting, particularly in tests:

config.i18n.raise_on_missing_translations = True

Fallbacks are disabled by default. Set config.i18n.fallbacks = True to look up missing keys in the configured default locale. Regional fallback chains and per-locale fallback mappings are not implemented. Defaults and fallback translations still support interpolation. Invalid locales always raise InvalidLocale, rather than falling back silently.

items.title: Select the request locale
items.text:
Like Rails, Flaskteroids leaves the selection policy to the application. It does not automatically trust a query parameter, cookie, or Accept-Language header. Use an around callback in ApplicationController to choose and restore the locale:

from flask import current_app

from flaskteroids.actions import around_action
from flaskteroids.controller import Controller
from flaskteroids.i18n import InvalidLocale, with_locale


class ApplicationController(Controller):
    def _switch_locale(self):
        selected = self.params.get("locale") or current_app.config.i18n.default_locale
        try:
            with with_locale(selected):
                yield
        except InvalidLocale:
            self.head(400)

    around_action("_switch_locale")

with_locale restores the previous locale after success, errors, redirects, and nested scopes. Locale state is isolated between requests, application contexts, and concurrent execution contexts. Each new request starts at its application's default, even if its caller has selected another locale.

Preserve a query-based choice explicitly in generated links:

{{ link_to("Español", products_path(locale="es")) }}

Route helpers accept query options, but do not automatically propagate the locale. New layouts set <html lang="{{ get_locale() }}">; add this to existing layouts when adopting internationalization.

items.title: Pluralization
items.text:
A translation can contain alternatives selected by count:

en:
  inbox:
    zero: "No messages"
    one: "One message"
    other: "%{count} messages"

t("inbox", count=0)  # No messages
t("inbox", count=1)  # One message
t("inbox", count=5)  # 5 messages

The basic rule follows Rails' simple backend: use zero for zero when provided, one when the count equals one, and other otherwise. Counts must be finite integers, floats, or Decimal values, not booleans or numeric strings. Missing plural forms raise TranslationError.

This basic rule is not linguistically correct for every language. Register a callable for each locale requiring different rules in application configuration:

def japanese_plural(count):
    return "other"


# Inside Application.configure:
config.i18n.pluralization_rules = {"ja": japanese_plural}

Enable ja in available_locales and provide other entries in its catalog. Callables return a catalog form key such as one, few, many, or other. An explicit zero entry still takes precedence at zero. Applications own these rules; Flaskteroids does not bundle comprehensive language-specific plural data. Fallback translations use the rule belonging to the locale that supplied them. Word inflection (person → people) remains separate from message selection.

items.title: HTML translations
items.text:
Ordinary translations and interpolated values are escaped by Jinja:

en:
  greeting: "<strong>Hello %{name}</strong>"
  greeting_html: "<strong>Hello %{name}</strong>"

{{ t("greeting", name=user.name) }}
{{ t("greeting_html", name=user.name) }}

The first prints literal HTML text. In an autoescaped HTML template, keys ending in _html, or whose last segment is html, allow application-authored markup. Interpolated values are still escaped unless explicitly trusted Markup values are supplied. Never mark user input trusted. Literal default= strings are escaped.

Catalog HTML is trusted application source, not sanitized user content. This convention does not validate links or make translations safe inside JavaScript, CSS, or URL attributes. Use it in HTML text content.

Python/controller translations return ordinary strings, even for _html keys. Text templates interpolate plain text without HTML escaping. Do not use |safe to make ordinary translations render as HTML.

items.title: Localize dates and times
items.text:
Use localize or its alias l in Python, controllers, or templates:

from datetime import date

from flaskteroids.i18n import l

l(date(2026, 3, 2))  # 2026-03-02 in English
l(date(2026, 3, 2), format="long")  # March 02, 2026

{{ l(product.created_at, format="short") }}

English includes default, short, and long formats and calendar names. Supply other languages in the application catalog:

es:
  date:
    formats:
      default: "%d/%m/%Y"
      long: "%-d de %B de %Y"
    month_names: [null, enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre]
  time:
    formats:
      default: "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M"
      short: "%H:%M"

Dates use date.formats; both datetime and time use time.formats. For a time-only object, provide a time-only format such as format="%H:%M" or a matching named format; the default English time formats include dates. A format= containing % is used directly instead of looking up a named format.

Use familiar directives such as %Y, %m, %d, %H, and %M. Month and day names come from date.month_names, date.abbr_month_names, date.day_names, and date.abbr_day_names in the catalog. Month arrays start with null; day arrays start with Sunday.

Formatting preserves the value's timezone; it does not convert timezones. Missing names or formats raise MissingTranslation. Process-locale formats such as %c, %x, and %X are not supported; define a named format in the catalog instead.

items.title: Mail and jobs
items.text:
Compose a mailer action inside the desired locale:

with with_locale("es"):
    NoticesMailer().welcome(user).deliver_later()

The message captures the locale when mail() is called, alongside its recipients and subject. Both immediate and queued delivery render templates and mailer helpers in that locale, restoring the delivery context afterward. Mail subjects can use t(...) from Python; mail templates use the same Jinja helpers as controller views. A relative key in notices_mailer/welcome.html resolves under notices_mailer.welcome.

General jobs do not yet capture locale automatically. Pass it as an ordinary job argument and use with_locale(locale) inside perform. Do not assume a worker inherits the request's locale.

items.title: What is translated
items.text: The helpers translate application messages and format dates and times. They do not yet translate built-in validation messages, model or attribute names, form labels, or generated scaffold text. Localized template variants and number or currency formatting are not included.

items.title: Background jobs
items.text:
Use a job for work that should happen outside an HTTP request, such as processing an upload. The web process enqueues the job; a separate worker runs it.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Define a job and enqueue it from your application.
  • Start a worker and configure its broker.
  • Test scheduling without running a worker.

items.title: Define and enqueue a job
items.text:
Jobs inherit from Job and define perform. Put the class under app/jobs so Flaskteroids registers it automatically:

# app/jobs/my_job.py
from flaskteroids.jobs.job import Job


class MyJob(Job):
    def perform(self, user_id):
        print(f"Performing job for user {user_id}")

Create an instance and call perform_later to enqueue it:

from app.jobs.my_job import MyJob

MyJob().perform_later(user_id=1)

This schedules the work; it does not run perform in the request. If the job needs newly saved records, enqueue it after the database transaction commits so the worker can read them.

items.title: Start a worker
items.text:
Celery is the default queue adapter. From the application directory, start a worker in a separate terminal:

bin/jobs start

The script uses the application's .venv and works from outside the application directory too. Run bin/setup first if the environment is missing. Extra options are passed to the Celery worker, for example:

bin/jobs start --concurrency=2 --loglevel=debug

The web process and worker must use the same environment and broker settings. See your generated Procfile and deploy/README.md for process examples.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Set config.jobs in application or environment configuration:

config.jobs.broker_url = "sqla+sqlite:///storage/jobs_database.db"
config.jobs.result_backend = None
config.jobs.additional_config = {}

The local SQLite broker is useful for development. For production, configure a broker accessible to both the web process and workers.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
Generated test configuration uses an in-memory adapter, so tests do not need a running worker or broker. To configure that adapter explicitly:

from flaskteroids.testing import TestQueueAdapter

config.jobs.queue_adapter = TestQueueAdapter

Use assert_enqueued_with to check scheduling and perform_enqueued_jobs to run jobs enqueued inside its block. See Testing.

items.title: Registration and application context
items.text: Enqueue jobs inside an application context. Requests already provide one, and workers run jobs in one. For scripts, open a context as shown in Configuration.

items.title: Mailers
items.text:
Mailers build and send email. Each action chooses a recipient and subject, and sets the values its templates need. You can deliver the message immediately or send it through a background job.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Create an email with text and HTML templates.
  • Preview it locally and deliver it in a background job.
  • Configure delivery and test the message.

items.title: Create a mailer
items.text:
Generate the mailer and its templates:

bin/flask generate mailer User welcome_email

Add the recipient and template values to the generated class:

# app/mailers/user_mailer.py
from app.mailers.application_mailer import ApplicationMailer


class UserMailer(ApplicationMailer):
    def welcome_email(self):
        self.user = self.params["user"]
        return self.mail(to=self.user.email, subject="Welcome to My App!")

Application mailers inherit from ApplicationMailer, whose base is the framework's Mailer. Templates match the mailer and action names:

<!-- app/views/user_mailer/welcome_email.html -->
<p>Welcome, {{ user.name }}!</p>

Use app/views/user_mailer/welcome_email.txt for the plain-text part. Text and HTML parts can be included in the same email.

items.title: Previewing and testing mailers
items.text: Previews let you inspect an email in your browser without sending it. Automated tests check its content and delivery behavior. Both use the same mailer and templates as your application.

items.title: Preview emails
items.text:
The mailer generator creates test/mailers/previews/user_mailer_preview.py alongside your mailer and tests. Update that file to call the UserMailer from above with sample data:

# test/mailers/previews/user_mailer_preview.py
from app.mailers.user_mailer import UserMailer
from app.models.user import User
from flaskteroids.mailer import MailerPreview


class UserMailerPreview(MailerPreview):
    def welcome_email(self):
        user = User(name="Jane", email="jane@example.com")
        return UserMailer.with_params(user=user).welcome_email()

A preview method returns the message; it does not call deliver_now() or deliver_later(). No SMTP server, job worker, or enabled delivery is needed.

Start the development server:

bin/flask run --debug

Visit http://localhost:5000/flaskteroids/mailers/user_mailer/welcome_email to see the rendered message. Open http://localhost:5000/flaskteroids/mailers for a list of all previews. The browser shows the sender, recipient, and subject, and lets you switch between HTML and plain text. API-only applications have the same preview browser.

Edit app/views/user_mailer/welcome_email.html and refresh to see the change. Generated development configuration enables template reloading; Flask's --debug reloader picks up changes to the mailer and preview Python files. Without --debug, restart the server after changing Python code.

The example uses an unsaved record so it works without creating data. You can also query existing development records when a scenario needs them. Previews do not load test fixtures.

items.title: Preview scenarios
items.text:
Add another method to the same preview class to inspect a different case:

def welcome_email_with_long_name(self):
    user = User(
        name="A particularly long display name",
        email="jane@example.com",
    )
    return UserMailer.with_params(user=user).welcome_email()

This scenario appears in the index and at /flaskteroids/mailers/user_mailer/welcome_email_with_long_name. Scenario names do not have to match mailer action names.

items.title: Preview parameters
items.text:
Query-string values are available as strings in self.params. For example, replace welcome_email with:

def welcome_email(self):
    user = User.find(self.params["user_id"])
    return UserMailer.with_params(user=user).welcome_email()

Visit /flaskteroids/mailers/user_mailer/welcome_email?user_id=123, using the ID of an existing development user. Each request gets a fresh preview instance and parameter dictionary. Switching formats preserves query parameters; part=html and part=plain are reserved for the browser's format selection.

items.title: Preview discovery
items.text:
Files ending in _preview.py are discovered recursively under test/mailers/previews. No routes or registration are needed. A file under previews/admin/ adds an admin/ prefix to its preview URLs. Class names drop the Preview suffix and become snake case.

Each public method defined directly on a MailerPreview subclass is a scenario. Methods take no arguments beyond self and must return a mailer's MessageDelivery. Use underscore-prefixed methods for shared helpers; inherited methods are not listed unless overridden. Rendering uses the normal mailer callbacks, template helpers, and captured locale.

items.title: Preview configuration
items.text:
Previews are enabled by default only in the development environment. To add another preview directory, append it in your application configuration:

config.mailer.preview_paths.append("lib/mailer_previews")

Paths are relative to the application root; absolute paths also work. Assign a new list to preview_paths to replace the default directories instead.

To disable previews in an environment, set this in its configure(config) function:

config.mailer.show_previews = False

None selects the environment default. Set show_previews = True to explicitly enable previews elsewhere, such as a test application. When disabled, preview files are not imported and the routes are absent.

Do not expose previews publicly or enable them in production. Preview routes do not run application controller authentication. Preview methods and mailer callbacks are ordinary application code: avoid writes, delivery calls, and other side effects. The browser does not undo those effects. Email HTML is isolated in a sandboxed frame, but the preview is not an email-client compatibility test.

items.title: Test mailers
items.text:
Preview files are support code, not automated tests. The generator separately creates test/mailers/user_mailer_test.py, inheriting from MailerTest. Run it with:

bin/flask test test/mailers/user_mailer_test.py

Generated tests collect delivered messages in memory rather than using SMTP. See jobs and mail assertions for delivery counts, queued jobs, and inspecting messages through self.deliveries.

items.title: Configure delivery
items.text:
Sending is disabled by default. Set delivery options in application or environment configuration. For an SMTP server that supports STARTTLS and authentication:

config.mailer.perform_deliveries = True
config.mailer.default_options = {"by": "hello@example.com"}
config.mailer.smtp_settings = {
    "host": "smtp.example.com",
    "port": 587,
    "username": "your-username",
    "password": "your-password",
}

These credentials are placeholders. Keep real secrets in encrypted credentials or your deployment's secret management, not source control. SMTP is the default delivery method; config.mailer.delivery_method can select another adapter.

The by option sets the email's From header. Pass it to mail() to override the configured default for an individual message:

return self.mail(
    to=self.user.email,
    by="team@example.com",
    subject="Welcome to My App!",
)

Generated tests use an in-memory mail adapter instead of SMTP. See mail assertions.

items.title: Send a message
items.text:
from app.mailers.user_mailer import UserMailer

UserMailer.with_params(user=user).welcome_email().deliver_now()
UserMailer.with_params(user=user).welcome_email().deliver_later()

deliver_now() sends in the current process. deliver_later() enqueues work; a job worker must be running to deliver it.

items.title: Pass data to a mailer
items.text:
with_params(...) supplies values through self.params. It does not need an HTTP request. Each action gets a fresh mailer instance and a shallow copy of the parameters. Actions can also accept ordinary arguments.

Parameters do not automatically become template variables. Assign them explicitly as instance variables, such as self.user in the example above.

items.title: Understand queued delivery
items.text:
Mail captures the locale when mail() is called and uses it for immediate or queued template rendering. See Internationalization for locale selection and translated subjects.

For queued messages, understand what is captured now and what is loaded later:

When What happens The action is called Actions and callbacks run; the recipient, subject, and template values are captured deliver_now() Templates render using the supplied objects deliver_later() Saved model values are serialized as record references The worker delivers Model references are reloaded and templates render; the action does not run again

Model references also work inside lists, tuples, and dictionaries. Other queued values must be serializable by the queue adapter.

Enqueue after commit so the worker can see the records. Unsaved models raise SerializationError on enqueue. A referenced record missing at delivery raises DeserializationError. Both exceptions are in flaskteroids.exceptions.

Queued rendering ignores unsaved edits without changing the caller's objects. Model-backed template content can therefore change before delivery, while the captured recipient and subject stay fixed. Text and HTML parts share one restored delivery-time mailer instance.

items.title: Mailer helper methods
items.text:
Use helper_method to expose a private method to mailer templates:

from app.mailers.application_mailer import ApplicationMailer
from flaskteroids.mailer import helper_method


class NoticesMailer(ApplicationMailer):
    helper_method("_greeting")

    def welcome(self, name, email):
        self.name = name
        return self.mail(to=email, subject="Welcome")

    def _greeting(self, punctuation="!"):
        return f"Hello, {self.name}{punctuation}"

<!-- app/views/notices_mailer/welcome.html -->
<p>{{ greeting() }}</p>

The declaration is inherited, honors child overrides, and forwards positional and keyword arguments. Private methods are not actions or template helpers unless explicitly exposed. Ordinary returned text is HTML-escaped.

Use helper(...) for a different task: including presentation helper classes in the view context. Those helpers can call exposed methods such as self.greeting(). Mailers select helper classes explicitly; they do not inherit request-controller helpers. See mailer view helpers.

items.title: Application middleware
items.text:
Middleware wraps the whole application before routing and controller callbacks. Use it for concerns that apply to every request, such as adding a response header or handling a trusted reverse proxy.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Write and register WSGI middleware.
  • Change its place in the request stack.
  • Inspect the stack used by your application.

Use controller callbacks instead when the behavior needs controller state or a browser session.

items.title: Write and register middleware
items.text:
Create app/middleware/security_headers.py:

class SecurityHeaders:
    def __init__(self, app, *, policy="nosniff"):
        self.app = app
        self.policy = policy

    def __call__(self, environ, start_response):
        def secured_response(status, headers, exc_info=None):
            headers = [*headers, ("X-Content-Type-Options", self.policy)]
            return start_response(status, headers, exc_info)

        return self.app(environ, secured_response)

Register it in config/application.py:

from app.middleware.security_headers import SecurityHeaders
from flaskteroids.application import Application as FlaskteroidsApplication
from config.boot import ROOT


class Application(FlaskteroidsApplication):
    root = ROOT

    def configure(self, config):
        config.load_defaults("0.1")
        config.middleware.use(SecurityHeaders, policy="nosniff")

The constructor receives the next WSGI application and your configured arguments. Its __call__ method delegates the request and adds a response header.

Middleware instances are shared across requests. Keep request-specific state in local variables or environ, not instance attributes. Middleware does not automatically have a Flask request or application context.

Delegate the response body unchanged unless you need to transform it. If you wrap the body, preserve its close() cleanup. Exceptions outside Flask dispatch are not handled by Flask error handlers.

items.title: Configure the stack
items.text:
The default incoming-request order is:

  1. Werkzeug's ProxyFix.
  2. MethodOverrideMiddleware in browser applications.
  3. Flask dispatch.

use() adds middleware just before Flask dispatch. Requests travel down the stack; response calls unwind in reverse. For a specific position, register your middleware relative to a class already in the stack:

from werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix import ProxyFix

from app.middleware.security_headers import SecurityHeaders

# Inside configure:
config.middleware.insert_after(ProxyFix, SecurityHeaders)

Use config.middleware.delete(SecurityHeaders) to remove it. Supply classes, not class-name strings. A missing insertion target fails at startup; deleting a missing target is harmless.

Environment configuration can also change config.middleware. The final stack is built after initializers; restart the application after changing it.

items.title: Trusted proxies
items.text:
Only trust forwarding headers when requests pass through the corresponding trusted proxies. Configure ProxyFix hop counts for your deployment:

from werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix import ProxyFix

# Inside configure; this example assumes one trusted proxy:
config.middleware.swap(ProxyFix, ProxyFix, x_for=1, x_proto=1)

Remove ProxyFix if proxy handling is not appropriate. See the Werkzeug ProxyFix documentation before choosing these values.

Removing MethodOverrideMiddleware disables browser form method overrides. API-only applications do not include it by default.

items.title: Inspect the stack
items.text:
From your application root, run:

bin/flask middleware

The command loads the application and lists middleware in incoming-request order, followed by Flask dispatch.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: See Configuration for environment settings, or Routing to follow a request into a controller.

items.title: Rich text
items.text:
Add formatted text, images, and file attachments with a model declaration and a form field. Flaskteroids provides the Lexxy editor, storage integration, and safe HTML rendering.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Add a rich-text editor to a model-backed form.
  • Save and render formatted content safely.
  • Manage embedded files and test the editor.

items.title: Set up
items.text:
Browser applications include flaskteroids-lexxy. Install rich text:

bin/flask generate scaffold Post title:string content:rich_text
bin/flask rich_text:install
bin/flask db:migrate

Restart the server, then visit /posts. The scaffold includes the declaration, editor, permitted parameters, display templates, and fixtures.

The installer generates shared rich_texts storage and, if not already installed, the attachment tables and config/storage.yml. It configures import-map pins, imports "flaskteroids/rich-text" in app/javascript/application.js, and adds {{ rich_text_assets() }} to app/views/layouts/application.html for styles. The runtime and stylesheets come from flaskteroids-lexxy; they are not copied into the application. No Node, npm, or editor CDN is required. Custom layouts need that stylesheet helper, {{ javascript_importmap_tags() }}, and the CSRF token meta tag in their <head>. See Import maps.

Repeated installation preserves existing files and avoids duplicate migrations. Production assets are built with bin/flask assets:precompile; generated Docker builds already do this. See upgrading the editor when refreshing an existing installation.

items.title: Model declarations
items.text:
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_rich_text, validates


class Post(ApplicationModel):
    has_rich_text("content")
    has_rich_text("summary", store_if_blank=False)
    validates("title", presence=True)
    validates("content", presence=True)

There is no content column on posts. Existing text columns need an explicit data migration and column removal before switching to a rich-text declaration. Owners require a single integer id primary key. Renaming a model also requires migrating its rich_texts.record_type values.

items.title: Assignment and rich-text records
items.text:
post = Post.new(title="Hello", content="<div>Hello <strong>world</strong></div>")
post.save()
post.content = "<div>Revised</div>"
post.save()

post.content is a RichText record, not a plain string. Its body is an immutable Content value: replace it rather than editing it in place. You can assign the attribute directly, as above, or assign its body. Both are saved when you save the owning Post:

post.content.body = "<em>Another revision</em>"
post.save()

assert post.rich_text_content is post.content
assert post.content.record is post

Assignment does not publish changes to unrelated saves. Failed validation retains the body and uploaded attachments for correction and form redisplay. Saves join the owner's transaction; destroying the owner destroys its rich-text rows and schedules dependent attachment cleanup.

Reading an unset attribute builds an empty rich-text record in memory. Reading alone does not write to the database. post.reload() discards submitted body changes and reloads persisted content.

items.title: Forms and parameters
items.text:
{% call(form) form_with(model=post) %}
  {{ form.label("title") }}
  {{ form.text_field("title") }}
  {{ form.label("content") }}
  {{ form.rich_text_area("content", placeholder="Write something…") }}
  {{ form.submit("Save") }}
{% endcall %}

Lexxy is a native form-associated control with an escaped initial HTML value, model prefixes, accessible labels, normal CSRF protection, and validation redisplay. Permit the body as a scalar:

def _post_params(self):
    return self.params.expect(post=["title", "content"])

Model-backed forms include a signed upload token tied to the browser session, plus a CSRF token. The editor supports file selection, drag-and-drop, and pasted images. Submission waits for uploads to finish, including when using Turbo. If an upload fails, an alert appears and submission is blocked until it is removed or retried. Standalone editors without the model-backed upload token do not accept attachments.

Lexxy supports semantic headings, lists, tables, inline formatting, code blocks with syntax highlighting, and color highlights. The server preserves these formats while rejecting executable markup and arbitrary layout styles. External images are disabled: upload images through the editor instead.

items.title: Rendering and attachments
items.text:
{{ post.content }}

This renders sanitized HTML inside <div class="lexxy-content">. Do not add |safe or wrap user input in Markup. The server sanitizes content regardless of whether it came from Lexxy or another request source.

Embedded attachments use verified, purpose-specific blob signatures. The server ignores client-supplied file URLs, filenames, types, sizes, and executable HTML; it resolves metadata from storage. Unverified or missing attachments are removed. Attachment captions, alternative text, and safe image links survive editing. Adjacent raster image previews render as a gallery. Other files render as download links. Active formats such as SVG and HTML use the existing attachment system's forced-download policy.

Programmatic attachment insertion uses the same storage API:

from flaskteroids.attachments import Blob

with open("photo.png", "rb") as stream:
    photo = Blob.create_and_upload(io=stream, filename="photo.png")

post.content.body = post.content.body.append_attachables([photo])
post.save()
post.content.embeds.blobs

embeds exposes the usual attachment collection operations. Normally, remove an embed by editing the body and saving it. Removed embeds and destroyed owners schedule purging after commit. Shared blobs remain until their final attachment is removed. Run the job worker to process purge jobs.

For a plain-text excerpt, use post.content.to_plain_text(). For HTML display, render the attribute itself so the sanitized output is marked safe correctly.

items.title: Upload permissions, limits, and private files
items.text:
The upload token is issued when your controller renders the form, so authorize access to that form. Upload routes do not run application controller callbacks. If permissions must be checked again at upload time, configure a callback in an initializer:

from flask import current_app
from app.helpers.permissions import can_upload_rich_text

# Callable(model_class, record_id_or_none, attribute_name) -> bool
current_app.config.rich_text.authorize_upload = can_upload_rich_text

Forms for new records pass None as the record ID. Upload tokens expire after an hour; change config.rich_text.upload_token_expires_in if needed.

Uploads honor config.attachments.max_upload_size and Flask's MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH. Set limits for your deployment. Rich-text encryption does not encrypt uploaded file bytes, and content-type checks do not replace malware scanning.

Downloads and image previews use the existing attachment routes and config.attachments.authorize callback. For private files, use proxy routing. An embed's attachment has record_type == "RichText"; its owner is accessible through RichText.find(attachment.record_id).record. A callback that authorizes only already-attached blobs will also deny previews of new draft uploads. Account for draft-upload access explicitly in your permission policy if needed; upload authorization does not bypass download authorization.

Anyone holding a signed attachment reference may reuse it, just as with an ordinary signed blob ID. Share these references only with users allowed to reuse the files. See Attachments for storage services, private downloads, and limits.

items.title: Abandoned uploads
items.text:
Uploads from abandoned forms remain unattached so failed validation does not destroy files awaiting resubmission. Schedule a job that calls:

Blob.purge_unattached()

This queues cleanup of all storage blobs that are unattached and older than two days, not only rich-text uploads. Set a positive older_than=timedelta(...) for another grace period. Purge jobs recheck attachments before deleting, so a file attached after the sweep is retained. Cleanup is not scheduled automatically.

items.title: Optional model behavior
items.text:
• store_if_blank=True (default): explicit blank assignment stores an empty body. With False, assigning None or blank HTML avoids creating an empty row. If a row already exists, it is removed on the model's next successful save. Omitting the attribute leaves it unchanged.
  • strict_loading=True: require content to be preloaded rather than issuing an extra query when accessed. Otherwise, StrictLoadingViolationError is raised. Use an eager-loading scope. New records and assigned bodies remain usable. The default comes from the model's strict_loading_by_default, normally False; it currently applies to rich text, not all ORM associations.
  • encrypted=True: transparently encrypts the stored body using a dedicated key; see Encryption.

Presence validation checks visible text and verified attachments. Formatting-only markup such as <div><br></div> is blank.

items.title: Eager loading
items.text:
Post.with_rich_text_content()             # Body record
Post.with_rich_text_content_and_embeds()  # Body, attachment metadata, and blobs
Post.where(title="Hello").with_rich_text_content_and_embeds()
Post.with_all_rich_text()                # All declared rich text and embeds

Preloading avoids extra queries when displaying several records. These methods return chainable model queries. Generated index actions already preload rich text and embedded attachments. For the body alone, you can also use Post.includes("rich_text_content"). With strict loading, rendering attachments requires an embed-loading scope. Rich-text attributes are not scalar columns and cannot be searched using Post.where(content=...).

items.title: Encryption
items.text:
Rich text uses the same attribute encryption service and dedicated keys as ordinary model attributes:

bin/flask db:encryption:init
bin/flask credentials:edit

Store the generated encryption YAML in encrypted credentials. The primary key encrypts rich-text bodies; neither the credentials master key nor the Flask signing secret is reused.

class Post(ApplicationModel):
    has_rich_text("content", encrypted=True)

Bodies use randomized, authenticated encryption. Missing/wrong keys, modified ciphertext, and unexpected plaintext raise EncryptionError by default. Editing and rendering still expose plaintext to the authorized application/browser. Rich text does not accept per-field deterministic encryption options.

For randomized-key rotation, configure config.encryption.primary_key = [previous_key, current_key]. The last key encrypts; all keys may decrypt. Re-encrypt before retiring old keys:

for post in Post.with_rich_text_content():
    post.content.encrypt()

The same explicit method migrates plaintext bodies after enabling encryption, without requiring permissive plaintext reads. Perform migrations before serving normal traffic; back up data and retain keys needed for old backups.

Encryption covers the body, not uploaded file bytes, attachment metadata, or rendered responses. Use storage-provider encryption and download authorization for files. Ciphertext uses Flaskteroids-specific envelopes.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
Scaffold fixtures accept HTML inline, including encrypted rich-text attributes:

one:
  title: Hello
  content: "<div>Hello <strong>world</strong></div>"

Configure test encryption keys when the declared field is encrypted. Fixtures use the normal rich-text persistence layer without running owner save callbacks.

self.fill_in_rich_text_area("Content", value="<div>Hello <strong>world</strong></div>")
self.click_on("Save")
self.assert_selector(".lexxy-content strong", text="world")

The helper fills HTML through Lexxy's public value property. Normal keyboard and file interaction remain available through the Playwright page.

items.title: Upgrade the editor
items.text:
Upgrade the locked Lexxy asset package independently:

uv lock --upgrade-package flaskteroids-lexxy
uv sync --locked
bin/flask assets:precompile

Commit the updated lockfile and deploy/restart the application. Generated Docker builds already precompile assets. Runtime upgrades do not require reinstalling rich text or changing its pins. Explicit application assets with the same logical names override packaged assets and remain application-owned.

The installer preserves application JavaScript, existing pins, layout content, and storage configuration. It reports manual setup instructions when pin configuration cannot be safely edited.

items.title: Limitations
items.text: Arbitrary record embeds, custom attachment-rendering partials, image resizing, video/PDF preview generation, and rich-text search are not implemented. RichText provides the record operations documented here, not the full Model API.

items.title: Add login and product images
items.text:
The catalog from Getting started lets anyone change products. In this part of the store tutorial, you will require login for changes and add a product photo to the existing form.

After working through this guide, you will know how to:

  • Generate a login workflow and keep browsing public.
  • Attach an image and accept it through a model-backed form.
  • Add styles and prepare assets for production.

Continue in the same store application, after completing Getting started. Keep the products you created there, and run commands from the application root.

items.title: Require login to change products
items.text:
Right now, anyone can create, edit, or delete products. Stop the server and run:

bin/flask generate authentication
bin/flask db:migrate

The generator adds User and Session models, login/logout and password-reset controllers, templates, mailers, routes, and tests. It also adds an Authentication concern to ApplicationController, making authentication the default for its subclasses. There is no public sign-up form.

Open bin/flask shell and create your own account:

from getpass import getpass

password = getpass("Choose a password: ")
user = User.create(
    email_address="you@example.org",
    password=password,
    password_confirmation=password,
)
assert not user.errors, user.errors.full_messages()
del password
exit()

has_secure_password() hashes the password; the database stores a digest, not its plaintext. Use a real password of your own, and do not put it in source code.

Restart the server and visit http://127.0.0.1:5000/products/new. You should be redirected to the login page at /session/new. Log in with your account.

items.title: Keep the catalog public
items.text:
Visitors should still be able to browse products without an account. In app/controllers/products_controller.py, add skip_before_action to the existing actions import:

from flaskteroids.actions import before_action, skip_before_action

Replace the existing callback declaration inside ProductsController with these two class-body calls, keeping its methods unchanged:

    skip_before_action("_require_authentication", only=["index", "show"])
    before_action("_set_product", only=["show", "edit", "update", "destroy"])

The generated Authentication concern provides the is_authenticated() template helper. It resumes the session when needed, including on public pages where _require_authentication is skipped. No extra callback or controller variable is needed.

items.title: Show login and logout controls
items.text:
Use the generated singular session resource for logout. Its session_path() destination accepts POST for login and DELETE for logout; button_to renders the browser-safe POST form, hidden DELETE override, and CSRF token. No extra logout endpoint or JavaScript is needed.

In app/views/products/index.html, replace the New product link with:

{% if is_authenticated() %}
  {{ link_to("New product", new_product_path()) }}
  {{ button_to("Log out", session_path(), method="DELETE") }}
{% else %}
  {{ link_to("Log in", new_session_path()) }}
{% endif %}

In app/views/products/show.html, wrap the Edit and Delete controls:

{% if is_authenticated() %}
  {{ link_to("Edit", edit_product_path(product)) }}
  {{ button_to("Delete", product, method="DELETE") }}
{% endif %}

Hiding controls is not access control: the controller callback protects the write actions even if someone sends a request directly. This example has one role: every account can manage the catalog. Ownership checks, permissions, and public registration need additional application rules.

Log out and verify that browsing still works, while /products/new requires login again. Password reset also needs working mail delivery before real users can rely on it.

Checkpoint: guests can browse the catalog, but only signed-in users can create, edit, or delete products. Keep the account you created: we'll use it to manage inventory shortly. We'll add automated checks after building the features.

items.title: Upload product images
items.text:
A shopper can browse the catalog, but an image makes a product easier to recognize. Let's add a photo without changing the product's ordinary edit flow. Install the attachment tables and configuration:

bin/flask attachments:install
bin/flask db:migrate

Stop and restart the server after this migration, as with other schema changes.

In app/models/product.py, import has_one_attached alongside validates, then update the declarations inside Product to:

    validates("name", presence=True)
    has_one_attached(
        "featured_image",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )

The attachment is not an extra column on products: the attachment tables keep track of files and their owning records.

Inside the form_with block in app/views/products/_form.html, before the submit button, add:

<div>
  {{ form.label("featured_image") }}
  {{ form.file_field("featured_image", accept="image/png,image/jpeg") }}
</div>

form_with detects the file field and adds multipart encoding. Permit the upload by replacing _product_params() in ProductsController with:

    def _product_params(self):
        return self.params.expect(product=["name", "description", "featured_image"])

In the body block of app/views/products/show.html, add:

{% if product.featured_image.attached() %}
  <img src="{{ blob_path(product.featured_image) }}" alt="{{ product.name }}">
{% endif %}

Log in, edit a product, and upload a small PNG or JPEG. After saving, its show page should display the image. Reopen Edit and save without selecting another file: the existing image should remain. Files become available after the save commits.

Development uses local disk storage. Signed download links are accessible to anyone who has the link by default, which suits public catalog images but not private documents. Content-type checks are not file scanning. See Attachments for storage services, authorization, request size limits, and cleanup jobs.

items.title: Give the store a little polish
items.text:
The generated layout already includes app/assets/stylesheets/application.css. Replace or extend that file with:

body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  max-width: 60rem;
  margin: 2rem auto;
  padding: 0 1rem;
}

form div {
  margin: 1rem 0;
}

label {
  display: block;
}

img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

.errors {
  color: #b91c1c;
}

Refresh a product page to see the change. Development serves source assets directly. Production uses fingerprinted files, built with:

bin/flask assets:precompile

Docker builds run this compilation automatically. Keep the generated output and manifest together; production has no fallback to source files.

The generated layout loads app/javascript/application.js through import maps. That entrypoint imports the local Turbo runtime supplied by the installed Flaskteroids package; no CDN or application-owned runtime copy is needed. Production precompilation fingerprints JavaScript like other assets. Add packages with bin/importmap pin PACKAGE; the compiler does not bundle JavaScript or compile Sass. See Import maps and Assets.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: You can now manage the catalog behind a login and display product photos. Continue with Restock notifications to connect associations, callbacks, background jobs, and email.

items.title: Prepare the store for deployment
items.text:
A working development application is a starting point for deployment, not a production configuration. This final part of the store tutorial explains what to review before you publish the application.

After working through this guide, you will know how to:

  • Run the store's tests in continuous integration.
  • Review the security boundaries used throughout the tutorial.
  • Check the generated Docker setup and identify the services production needs.

Continue with the store application from Test the store. The Docker example requires Docker; a real deployment also requires a hosting platform and its own service and secret configuration.

items.title: Security and continuous integration
items.text:
Before deploying, run the complete suite:

bin/flask test
bin/flask test:system

The generated .github/workflows/test.yml provides a starting CI workflow. Review it and keep your application's tests and browser dependencies up to date. Linting or security scanners you choose for your application need their own configuration.

Keep these boundaries in mind:

  • Use self.params.expect() allowlists, even when the browser form looks harmless.
  • Protect write actions on the server, not just their links in templates.
  • Keep CSRF protection enabled; form helpers include the required tokens.
  • Let Jinja and helpers escape user input. Never mark product descriptions safe merely to display formatting.
  • Keep master keys, passwords, database URLs, and SMTP credentials out of Git.
  • Do not expose the debug server to production traffic.
  • Configure HTTPS, upload limits, access policies, and backups for your deployment.

items.title: Prepare for production
items.text:
Flaskteroids generates a Dockerfile and deployment scripts. Start by reading your app's deploy/README.md, which contains the commands matching your generated application. You will need to choose and configure your own hosting platform.

For a local production-mode Docker check, commit your application lockfile and build an image:

docker build -t store .
docker volume create store-storage

Supply FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY at runtime using your secret manager. For a local check only, read the generated key into your shell and forward it to Docker:

export FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY="$(tr -d '\n' < config/master.key)"
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
  --env FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY \
  --volume store-storage:/app/storage \
  store

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. This is a separate production database, so it will not contain the development products or account you created earlier. Stop the container with Ctrl-C when finished and unset the key:

unset FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY

The default web startup prepares the production database before launching Gunicorn. The volume keeps SQLite data and local uploads across container restarts. The image runs unprivileged; host bind mounts must be writable by its application user.

For a real deployment:

  1. Provide the matching credentials key and environment settings through your hosting platform's secret management.
  2. Configure your database and install its driver if using PostgreSQL or MySQL.
  3. Coordinate migrations once per release when running multiple instances; do not use each web instance as migration coordination.
  4. Configure SMTP and a sender address for real mail, your canonical host via SERVER_NAME for email links, external storage if needed, and a Celery broker and worker. The tutorial's console adapter is only enabled in development.
  5. Put the application behind HTTPS and arrange persistent storage and backups.
  6. Create an initial user through an application shell in the production environment, using your host's execution facility and the account creation code from the login guide. Do not add credentials to the image or Git.

See Configuration and your generated deployment guide for release commands and service settings. The Docker check above is not a complete internet-facing deployment recipe.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
You started with an empty application and built a working store: visitors browse products, owners manage stock and images, and subscribers hear when a product returns. Tests now check the behavior that makes those features work together.

Next, try expanding it:

  • Add product categories with another model and association.
  • Add pagination and filtering to the catalog.
  • Confirm subscription addresses before enabling notifications for real visitors.
  • Write a browser test for the complete subscribe-and-unsubscribe journey.
  • Return JSON alongside HTML using controller content negotiation.

Explore the focused guides as you go:

  • Models: queries, transactions, associations, and callbacks.
  • Controllers and Routing.
  • Views and Forms.
  • Attachments, Mailers, and Background jobs.
  • Testing, Configuration, and CLI.

items.title: Add restock notifications
items.text:
Let visitors ask for an email when a sold-out product becomes available again. This part of the store tutorial follows one feature from its database tables to the email a subscriber receives.

After working through this guide, you will know how to:

  • Associate subscribers with products.
  • Accept public subscriptions and provide unsubscribe links.
  • Send a background email after inventory changes commit.

Continue in the store application from Add login and product images. You will use its login workflow and product form. Run commands from the application root.

items.title: Notify visitors when products return to stock
items.text: Our catalog can describe a product and show its image, but it cannot answer a shopper's next question: "Can I get one?" Let's track inventory. If a product sells out, visitors will be able to subscribe to a restock email and unsubscribe later.

items.title: Track inventory
items.text:
Stop the server and generate a migration for the existing products table:

bin/flask generate migration AddInventoryCountToProducts inventory_count:integer

Open the new file under db/migrate/versions/. In upgrade(), change only the inventory_count column to add nullable=False and server_default="0":

sa.Column("inventory_count", sa.Integer(), nullable=False, server_default="0")

Keep the rest of the migration unchanged. The default gives existing and new products a count of zero; nullable=False prevents null values. These are inventory-specific choices, not defaults the generator can infer.

Apply it:

bin/flask db:migrate

Replace app/models/product.py with the following, preserving the attachment declaration we added earlier:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_one_attached, validates


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    validates("name", presence=True)
    validates("inventory_count", numericality={"only_integer": True})
    validates("inventory_count", comparison={"greater_than_or_equal_to": 0})
    has_one_attached(
        "featured_image",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )

The database supplies the default; validations explain invalid user input. Both inventory_count declarations apply: repeated validates calls add checks rather than replacing earlier ones.

Add this field before the submit button in app/views/products/_form.html:

<div>
  {{ form.label("inventory_count") }}
  {{ form.number_field("inventory_count") }}
</div>

Replace _product_params() in ProductsController so edits can include stock:

    def _product_params(self):
        return self.params.expect(
            product=["name", "description", "featured_image", "inventory_count"]
        )

Create app/views/products/_inventory.html:

{% if product.inventory_count > 0 %}
  <p>{{ product.inventory_count }} in stock</p>
{% else %}
  <p>Out of stock</p>
{% endif %}

Include it after the description in app/views/products/show.html:

{% include "products/_inventory.html" %}

Restart the server. Try it: an existing product should say Out of stock. Log in, edit its inventory count to 5, and save: the page should say 5 in stock. Try -1 and check that the form explains the error and keeps the entered value. Finally set the count to 0 so we can build the subscription experience.

items.title: Remember who wants an email
items.text:
A product can have many subscribers, and each subscriber belongs to a product. Generate the subscriber model and its migration:

bin/flask generate model Subscriber product:references email:string unsubscribe_token:string

The reference creates product_id and a foreign key. Open the generated CreateSubscribers migration and add this after op.create_table(...) in upgrade():

    op.create_index(
        "ix_subscribers_unsubscribe_token",
        "subscribers",
        ["unsubscribe_token"],
        unique=True,
    )

The generated downgrade() drops the table, including its index. Apply the migration:

bin/flask db:migrate

Replace app/models/subscriber.py with:

from secrets import token_urlsafe

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import before_create, belongs_to, validates


class Subscriber(ApplicationModel):
    belongs_to("product")
    validates("email", presence=True)
    before_create("_assign_unsubscribe_token")

    def _assign_unsubscribe_token(self):
        self.unsubscribe_token = token_urlsafe(32)

A before_create callback assigns a random token before the record is first saved. That token will let someone unsubscribe without an account. Treat it like a credential: do not expose a subscriber list or log the tokens.

In app/models/product.py, add has_many to the existing model import and add has_many("subscribers", dependent="destroy") inside the model class. Deleting a product will now delete its subscriptions too.

Restart the server, then open bin/flask shell:

>>> product = Product.find_by(name="Cotton T-Shirt")
>>> subscriber = Subscriber.create(product=product, email="reader@example.org")
>>> subscriber.product.name
'Cotton T-Shirt'
>>> [person.email for person in product.subscribers]
['reader@example.org']
>>> bool(subscriber.unsubscribe_token)
True

The association connects the objects without manually looking up a foreign-key value. Exit the shell. Next, let's let visitors do this from the product page.

items.title: Add the subscription form
items.text:
Create app/controllers/subscribers_controller.py:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.product import Product
from flaskteroids.actions import skip_before_action
from flaskteroids.routes import product_path


class SubscribersController(ApplicationController):
    skip_before_action("_require_authentication")

    def create(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["product_id"])
        self.subscriber = self.product.subscribers.where(
            **self.params.expect(subscriber=["email"])
        ).first_or_create()
        if not self.subscriber.is_persisted():
            return self.render("new", status=422)
        return self.redirect_to(
            product_path(self.product),
            notice="We will email you when it is back in stock.",
        )

Subscriptions are public, unlike editing stock. The email is allowlisted, and the product comes from the URL rather than an editable form field. Looking up an existing subscription through the product's association avoids adding another during ordinary repeat visits. first_or_create() returns the existing record or attempts to save a new one using the scope's email and parent. A rejected save returns its errors and entered values for redisplay. This lookup is not an atomic uniqueness guarantee; a production signup service also needs database constraints, confirmation, and abuse controls.

In config/routes.py, replace the existing route.resources("products") declaration with the nested resource, keeping your other routes:

    route.resources(
        "products",
        nested=lambda child: child.resources("subscribers", only=["create"]),
    )

Product member actions still receive id; subscriber creation receives product_id. Python and templates can both use product_subscribers_path(product).

The nested URL tells the controller which product the visitor wants to follow. Replace app/views/products/_inventory.html with:

{% if product.inventory_count > 0 %}
  <p>{{ product.inventory_count }} in stock</p>
{% else %}
  <p>Out of stock</p>
  <p>Email me when it is available:</p>
  {% call(form) form_with(model=[product, Subscriber.new()]) %}
    {{ form.email_field("email", required=True, placeholder="you@example.org") }}
    {{ form.submit("Notify me") }}
  {% endcall %}
{% endif %}

The final model determines field scope and values, so the email is named subscriber[email] automatically. The parent supplies the nested URL binding; it does not become the field prefix or enable nested-attribute persistence. The controller filters the child with self.params.expect(subscriber=["email"]).

Create app/views/subscribers/new.html for invalid submissions:

{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Follow {{ product.name }}</h1>
  <ul class="errors">
    {% for message in subscriber.errors.full_messages() %}
      <li>{{ message }}</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
  {% call(form) form_with(model=[product, subscriber]) %}
    {{ form.email_field("email", required=True) }}
    {{ form.submit("Notify me") }}
  {% endcall %}
  {{ link_to("Back", product_path(product)) }}
{% endblock %}

Our successful redirect sets a flash notice. In app/views/layouts/application.html, add this just after <body>, before the body block:

{% if flash.notice %}<p role="status">{{ flash.notice }}</p>{% endif %}
{% if flash.alert %}<p role="alert">{{ flash.alert }}</p>{% endif %}

Try it: log out, open an out-of-stock product, and subscribe with another email address. You should return to the product and see the confirmation. Subscribe with the same address again: the ordinary repeat request should still show confirmation, not create another record. In a new shell, select the product with product = Product.find_by(name="Cotton T-Shirt"), then check Subscriber.where(product_id=product.id).count().

items.title: Let subscribers leave
items.text:
Before sending notifications, let's give recipients a way to stop them. Add these routes inside register in config/routes.py:

    route.get("/unsubscribe/<token>/", to="unsubscribes#show", aka="unsubscribe")
    route.post(
        "/unsubscribe/<token>/", to="unsubscribes#destroy", aka="cancel_subscription"
    )

Create app/controllers/unsubscribes_controller.py:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.subscriber import Subscriber
from flaskteroids.actions import skip_before_action


class UnsubscribesController(ApplicationController):
    skip_before_action("_require_authentication")

    def show(self):
        self.subscriber = Subscriber.find_by(unsubscribe_token=self.params["token"])
        if self.subscriber is None:
            return self.redirect_to("/", notice="This subscription is no longer active.")

    def destroy(self):
        subscriber = Subscriber.find_by(unsubscribe_token=self.params["token"])
        if subscriber is not None:
            subscriber.destroy()
        return self.redirect_to("/", notice="You are unsubscribed.")

Create app/views/unsubscribes/show.html:

{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Stop following {{ subscriber.product.name }}?</h1>
  {% call(form) form_with(url=url_for("cancel_subscription", token=subscriber.unsubscribe_token)) %}
    {{ form.submit("Unsubscribe") }}
  {% endcall %}
{% endblock %}

Opening an email link displays a confirmation; only submitting its CSRF-protected POST form removes the subscription. Email link scanners therefore do not unsubscribe someone just by following a GET request. Invalid or already-used tokens redirect safely to the catalog.

items.title: Write the restock email
items.text:
Generate a mailer:

bin/flask generate mailer Product in_stock

Replace app/mailers/product_mailer.py with:

from app.mailers.application_mailer import ApplicationMailer


class ProductMailer(ApplicationMailer):
    def in_stock(self):
        self.product = self.params["product"]
        self.subscriber = self.params["subscriber"]
        return self.mail(
            to=self.subscriber.email,
            subject=f"{self.product.name} is back in stock",
        )

with_params(...) supplies the mailer's self.params, using the same API as controllers without an HTTP request. Instance variables expose the product and subscriber to templates; queued delivery reloads these saved records.

Email links need absolute URLs: product_url is the absolute counterpart of product_path. The custom unsubscribe endpoint still uses url_for with _external=True.

Replace app/views/product_mailer/in_stock.html with:

<h1>Good news!</h1>
<p>{{ link_to(product.name, product_url(product)) }} is back in stock.</p>
<p>{{ link_to("Unsubscribe", url_for("unsubscribe", token=subscriber.unsubscribe_token, _external=True)) }}</p>

Replace app/views/product_mailer/in_stock.txt with:

Good news! {{ product.name }} is back in stock.
{{ product_url(product) }}

Unsubscribe: {{ url_for("unsubscribe", token=subscriber.unsubscribe_token, _external=True) }}

items.title: Preview delivery locally
items.text:
We want to see the message without needing a real mailbox. Create app/mailers/console_delivery.py, an application-owned development adapter:

class ConsoleDeliveryMethod:
    def __init__(self, application, config):
        pass

    def deliver(self, message):
        print(f"To: {message['To']}", flush=True)
        print(f"Subject: {message['Subject']}", flush=True)
        print(message.get_body(preferencelist=("plain",)).get_content(), flush=True)

Replace config/environments/development.py with:

from app.mailers.console_delivery import ConsoleDeliveryMethod


def configure(config):
    config.enable_reloading = True
    config.consider_all_requests_local = True
    config.controller.perform_caching = False
    config.attachments.service = "local"
    config["SERVER_NAME"] = "127.0.0.1:5000"
    config.mailer.perform_deliveries = True
    config.mailer.delivery_method = ConsoleDeliveryMethod
    config.jobs.broker_url = "sqla+sqlite:///storage/jobs_database.db"

SERVER_NAME supplies a host for absolute links even in the shell. This adapter prints mail; it does not send real messages. The development queue uses a local SQLite file, so this example needs no separate broker server.

Restart the web server. Open a new bin/flask shell and preview one email:

from app.mailers.product_mailer import ProductMailer

subscriber = Subscriber.find_by(email="reader@example.org")
product = subscriber.product
ProductMailer.with_params(
    product=product, subscriber=subscriber
).in_stock().deliver_now()

You should see a readable message preview in the shell, with a subject ending in "is back in stock", a product link, and an unsubscribe link. Exit the shell. The action runs immediately; deliver_later() queues its captured template assigns, not self.params. See Mailers for delivery details.

items.title: Trigger notifications after a restock
items.text:
Now connect inventory to email. Replace app/models/product.py with:

from app.mailers.product_mailer import ProductMailer
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import (
    after_commit,
    has_many,
    has_one_attached,
    validates,
)


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    validates("name", presence=True)
    validates("inventory_count", numericality={"only_integer": True})
    validates("inventory_count", comparison={"greater_than_or_equal_to": 0})
    has_one_attached(
        "featured_image",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )
    has_many("subscribers", dependent="destroy")
    after_commit("_notify_subscribers", on="update", when="_back_in_stock")

    def _back_in_stock(self):
        change = self.saved_change_to_attribute("inventory_count")
        return change is not None and change[0] == 0 and change[1] > 0

    def _notify_subscribers(self):
        for subscriber in self.subscribers:
            ProductMailer.with_params(
                product=self, subscriber=subscriber
            ).in_stock().deliver_later()

saved_change_to_attribute() returns the old and new typed values from the latest successful save, or None when that attribute did not change. A change from zero to a positive count triggers one email per subscriber. An ordinary description edit or a change from 5 to 6 does not send a new batch.

after_commit runs only after the outer transaction commits, so a rollback never enqueues these notifications. The callback can query subscribers normally; the mailer captures each message's recipient and subject when called, while queued template models reload at delivery. If an explicit transaction saves the same product more than once, the condition describes its last successful save, not every intermediate transition. See Models for callbacks, saved changes, and transactions.

items.title: Watch the complete feature work
items.text:
Restart the web server to load the model. From store, start a worker in another terminal:

bin/jobs start

The web process and worker read the same development configuration and local queue. Keep both running for this checkpoint:

  1. Log in and set Cotton T-Shirt's inventory count to 0.
  2. Log out and subscribe from its product page with a second email address.
  3. Log in again, change the inventory count to 5, and save.
  4. Watch the worker terminal: one message per subscribed address should appear.
  5. Change the count from 5 to 6. There should be no new restock email.
  6. Copy an unsubscribe URL from a message into the browser and confirm removal.
  7. Set stock to 0 and then 5 again. That recipient should no longer get an email.

We now have a reason for every piece: inventory drives the page, associations remember interested visitors, callbacks notice a restock, and a mailer and job queue deliver the notification outside the request.

The console adapter is for development only. Real delivery needs SMTP settings and a sender address; production also needs a worker and a suitable shared broker when running multiple instances. Generated production settings read CELERY_BROKER_URL. See Mailers, Background jobs, and Configuration for those settings.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: The store now connects a visitor's subscription to a restock email. Continue with Test the store to check the behavior automatically.

items.title: Test the store
items.text:
You have tried the store in a browser. Now turn its main behaviors into automated checks, from saving a product to delivering a restock email.

After working through this guide, you will know how to:

  • Set up related records with fixtures.
  • Test models, email, and public request behavior.
  • Follow a signed-in user's journey in a browser test.

Continue in the store application after completing Restock notifications. The examples use its Subscriber model, inventory callbacks, and mailer. Run commands from the application root.

items.title: Test the store's behavior
items.text:
We have exercised the store in a browser. Let's turn its important behaviors into repeatable tests: valid products save, guests can subscribe but cannot edit, and restocking emails the right people.

Tests use a separate test environment and database. bin/flask test applies pending migrations and runs pytest-based tests. Framework test classes roll back their database changes between tests. The test mail and queue adapters keep messages in memory, so you do not need the development worker or real SMTP.

items.title: Give the tests a small catalog
items.text:
Create test/fixtures/products.yml:

shirt:
  name: T-Shirt
  description: A comfortable cotton shirt.
  inventory_count: 0

Create test/fixtures/subscribers.yml:

reader:
  product: shirt
  email: reader@example.org
  unsubscribe_token: reader-test-token

another:
  product: shirt
  email: another@example.org
  unsubscribe_token: another-test-token

Fixture labels connect subscribers to shirt without hard-coded IDs. These example tokens belong only to the test database; real subscriptions generate random ones. Declare both fixture sets in tests that need the association.

items.title: Test products and restock notifications
items.text:
Replace test/models/product_test.py with:

from test.test_helper import ModelTest

import pytest

from app.models.product import Product


class ProductTest(ModelTest):
    fixtures = ["products", "subscribers"]

    def test_save_persists_valid_product(self):
        product = Product.new(name="Socks", description="Warm socks.")

        assert product.save()
        assert Product.find(product.id).name == "Socks"

    def test_save_rejects_blank_name(self):
        product = Product.new(name="")

        assert not product.save()
        assert product.errors
        assert product.id is None

    def test_inventory_rejects_negative_input(self):
        product = Product.new(name="Socks", inventory_count=-1)

        assert not product.save()
        assert product.inventory_count == -1
        assert product.errors

    def test_restock_emails_subscribers(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")

        with self.assert_emails(2), self.perform_enqueued_jobs():
            assert product.update(inventory_count=5)

        assert {message["To"] for message in self.deliveries} == {
            "reader@example.org",
            "another@example.org",
        }

    def test_positive_stock_adjustment_preserves_notification_count(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")
        assert product.update(inventory_count=5)

        with self.assert_emails(0), self.perform_enqueued_jobs():
            assert product.update(inventory_count=6)

    def test_rolled_back_restock_keeps_queue_empty(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")

        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Cancel restock"):
            with Product.transaction():
                assert product.update(inventory_count=5)
                assert not self.enqueued_jobs
                raise ValueError("Cancel restock")

        assert not self.enqueued_jobs

The notification test changes stock from zero to five and performs jobs as they are enqueued. It checks the recipients as well as the count. The other cases check that ordinary stock adjustments and rolled-back updates do not produce restock notifications.

Run just these tests:

bin/flask test test/models/product_test.py

You should see them pass without contacting a broker or mail server.

items.title: Check the actual email
items.text:
Replace the generated test/mailers/product_mailer_test.py with:

from test.test_helper import MailerTest

from app.mailers.product_mailer import ProductMailer


class ProductMailerTest(MailerTest):
    fixtures = ["products", "subscribers"]

    def test_email_contains_product_and_unsubscribe_links(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")
        subscriber = self.subscribers("reader")

        with self.assert_emails(1):
            ProductMailer.with_params(
                product=product, subscriber=subscriber
            ).in_stock().deliver_now()

        message = self.deliveries[0]
        assert message["To"] == subscriber.email
        assert message["Subject"] == "T-Shirt is back in stock"
        text = message.get_body(preferencelist=("plain",)).get_content()
        assert f"/products/{product.id}" in text
        assert f"/unsubscribe/{subscriber.unsubscribe_token}/" in text

items.title: Check guest access and subscriptions
items.text:
Replace test/controllers/products_controller_test.py with:

from test.test_helper import IntegrationTest, get, post

from app.models.subscriber import Subscriber
from flaskteroids.routes import new_product_path, new_session_path, products_path


class ProductsControllerTest(IntegrationTest):
    fixtures = ["products", "subscribers"]

    def test_guest_can_browse_products(self):
        get(products_path())

        self.assert_response("success")

    def test_guest_is_redirected_to_login(self):
        get(new_product_path())

        self.assert_redirected_to(new_session_path())

    def test_guest_can_subscribe_to_product(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")

        with self.assert_difference(Subscriber.count):
            post(
                f"/products/{product.id}/subscribers",
                params={"subscriber": {"email": "new-reader@example.org"}},
            )

        assert Subscriber.find_by(
            product_id=product.id, email="new-reader@example.org"
        )

    def test_unsubscribe_link_requires_confirmation(self):
        subscriber = self.subscribers("reader")
        path = f"/unsubscribe/{subscriber.unsubscribe_token}/"

        with self.assert_difference(Subscriber.count, by=0):
            get(path)
