        self.assert_response("success")

        with self.assert_difference(Subscriber.count, by=-1):
            post(path)
        self.assert_redirected_to("/")

The request helpers simulate HTTP without starting a web server. Checking both GET and POST makes the unsubscribe boundary explicit: following the email link is safe; confirming the form removes the subscription.

items.title: Walk through an edit in a real browser
items.text:
Create test/system/products_test.py:

from test.test_helper import SystemTest

from app.models.user import User
from flaskteroids.routes import new_product_path


class ProductsTest(SystemTest):
    def setup(self):
        User.create(
            email_address="owner@example.org",
            password="test-password-only",
            password_confirmation="test-password-only",
        )

    def test_owner_creates_and_edits_product(self):
        self.visit(new_product_path())
        self.page.get_by_placeholder("Enter your email address").fill("owner@example.org")
        self.page.locator('input[name="password"]').fill("test-password-only")
        self.click_on("Sign in")
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="New product")

        self.fill_in("Name", value="Browser hat")
        self.fill_in("Description", value="A hat created in the browser.")
        self.click_on("Save product")
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="Browser hat")

        self.click_on("Edit")
        self.fill_in("Name", value="Updated browser hat")
        self.click_on("Save product")
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="Updated browser hat")

The test follows the login flow rather than constructing a session cookie. Its password is fixed test data, not an account used in development or production. Browser tests use Playwright. Install Chromium once, then run the suite:

.venv/bin/playwright install chromium
bin/flask test:system

You should see the browser journey pass. Run all non-browser tests too:

bin/flask test

The generated health and authentication tests should pass alongside the tests we wrote. You now have checks for the whole story, from editing a product to subscribing and delivering its restock email. See Testing for uploads, additional assertions, and running selected tests in parallel.

items.text: You now have repeatable checks for the store's main workflows. Continue with Prepare the store for deployment to review security, continuous integration, and production setup.

items.title: Views
items.text:
Views are Jinja templates in app/views. They turn the data prepared by a controller into HTML.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Render a page and extract reusable partials.
  • Share presentation logic through helper classes.
  • Keep template output escaped.

items.title: Render a page
items.text:
By default, controller and action names choose the template. PostsController.index renders app/views/posts/index.html. Values assigned by the action become template variables, so self.posts is available as posts.

<!-- app/views/posts/index.html -->
{% extends layout %}

{% block body %}
<h1>Posts</h1>

<ul>
  {% for post in posts %}
  <li>{{ post.title }}</li>
  {% endfor %}
</ul>
{% endblock %}

items.title: Render a partial
items.text:
A partial is a template you can reuse inside another template. Put a post's display markup in app/views/posts/_post.html:

<article>
  <h2>{{ post.title }}</h2>
</article>

Render it with a local value:

{{ render(partial="posts/post", locals={"post": post}) }}

With conventional names, {{ render(post) }} selects the same partial and supplies post automatically. The template helper returns HTML; it is different from a controller's self.render(...), which prepares an HTTP response.

items.title: Turbo Frames and Streams
items.text: Use Turbo Frames and Streams to navigate within a page or update several elements after a form submission. Page templates use {% extends layout %} so the controller can select a full-page or frame layout.

items.title: Translations and dates
items.text: Use t("products.index.title") for translations and l(value, format="short") for localized dates and times. A relative key such as t(".title") uses the current template context. See Internationalization for YAML catalogs, locale selection, pluralization, and safe HTML translations.

items.title: Application helpers
items.text:
Put reusable presentation methods in helper classes under app/helpers. The application generator creates ApplicationHelper; the controller generator also creates a matching helper class.

For example:

# app/helpers/products_helper.py
class ProductsHelper:
    def product_link(self, product):
        return self.link_to(product.name, self.product_path(product))

Use it directly in a view, layout, or partial:

{{ product_link(product) }}

By default, all conventional helper classes are available in every controller's views. No import, callback, or helper_method declaration is needed.

items.title: Discovery and the view context
items.text:
Helper files follow a naming convention: products_helper.py defines ProductsHelper. Put shared methods in ApplicationHelper. All conventional helper classes are included in controller views by default.

A helper runs on a view context, not the controller. Within a helper, use self to call other helpers, route helpers, or explicitly exposed controller methods. Pass template-local values as arguments.

Public methods are available in templates; underscore-prefixed methods remain private to helpers. Do not define __init__. Any state you create is shared by the current view, layout, and partials, but not by separate renders or requests.

items.title: Restricting automatic inclusion
items.text:
To include shared application helpers and only conventionally matching controller helpers, configure:

config.controller.include_all_helpers = False

For example, ProductsController receives ApplicationHelper and ProductsHelper. Child controllers inherit their parents' helper selections and add their own matching helper. Namespaced controllers match namespaced helper paths.

Include other helper classes explicitly inside the controller class:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.helpers.formatting_helper import FormattingHelper
from flaskteroids.controller import helper


class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    helper(FormattingHelper, "admin/money")

Names such as "formatting", "FormattingHelper", and "admin/money" resolve against the configured helper package. helper("all") explicitly includes all discovered helpers.

helper(...) includes presentation helpers in the view context; helper_method(...) delegates a particular method to the current controller or delivery-time mailer.

items.title: Method precedence
items.text: Prefer unique helper method names. When names overlap, later includes override earlier ones, and a child controller's helpers can override inherited helpers. Use ordinary Python super() when extending an inherited helper method.

items.title: Mailers and rendering outside requests
items.text:
Mailer templates do not inherit the current request controller's helper methods or automatically include every application helper. Include the classes they need explicitly:

from app.mailers.application_mailer import ApplicationMailer
from flaskteroids.mailer import helper


class NoticesMailer(ApplicationMailer):
    helper("application", "formatting")
    # Mailer actions go here.

A conventionally matching NoticesMailerHelper, if defined in notices_mailer_helper.py, is also included. Mailer instance variables are available to helpers through self. These selections apply to immediate and queued delivery. Mailers can also expose their own private methods with helper_method, imported from flaskteroids.mailer. These declarations are inherited, honor overridden methods, and accept arguments just like controller helper methods. They delegate to the mailer, never to a request controller.

See Mailers for delivery-time values and helper methods.

items.title: Rendering without a controller
items.text: Flask template rendering inside an application context uses all application helpers by default, or just ApplicationHelper when include_all_helpers is false. Controller delegates are unavailable without a current request controller. Request-dependent helpers still require a request; URL generation outside a request follows Flask's normal configuration rules. Jinja macros imported without context do not receive render-local helpers; import them with context when needed.

items.title: Development changes
items.text: Helper modules are imported at application boot. Use bin/flask run --debug for Flask's process reloader, or restart the server after changing Python helpers. The framework does not perform a separate in-process module reload. config.enable_reloading enables template reloading but does not, by itself, reload Python helper code.

items.title: Helper escaping and URLs
items.text:
Template output is HTML-escaped by default. Keep that protection when writing helpers: link_to() and button_to() escape ordinary text and attribute values. Use markupsafe.Markup only for HTML you trust, such as an application-defined icon or label. Never mark user input safe. Attributes are escaped even when supplied as Markup.

link_to() accepts relative URLs, including protocol-relative URLs, and the http, https, mailto, and tel schemes. Form helpers accept relative and HTTP(S) action URLs. Unsupported schemes, such as javascript and data, and URLs containing control characters raise ValueError. HTML escaping alone does not make an executable URL safe.

link_to, button_to, form_with, and Turbo tag helpers accept class_="button" as class="button", nested data={"turbo_frame": "editor"} / aria={"label": "Edit"} dictionaries, and boolean HTML attributes. For example, disabled=True includes the boolean attribute; False omits it. Data/ARIA booleans instead emit "true" or "false".

These checks do not restrict destination hosts. Applications must validate user-supplied destinations when links or forms should stay on a particular site. Keep HTML attribute names application-defined. Invalid names raise ValueError; valid event-handler attributes still contain executable code and must never come from untrusted input.

items.title: Turbo Frames and Streams
items.text:
Turbo lets you update a page without writing JavaScript for each interaction. Use a Frame to replace one region during navigation, or an HTTP Stream response to change several elements after a request.

This guide starts with an inline post editor, then adds a form that appends a post to a list. It assumes a Post model with a title attribute and route.resources("posts"). Updates here are request-driven, not broadcasts or live subscriptions.

After reading this guide, you will know how to:

  • Edit a record inside a Turbo Frame.
  • Update several page elements with an HTTP Stream response.
  • Handle validation failures and cache responses safely.

items.title: Install or upgrade
items.text:
New browser applications include Turbo 8.0.23 through flaskteroids-turbo and load it through import maps, without a CDN or runtime download. The layout includes a CSRF meta token.

bin/flask turbo:install restores missing import-map conventions without replacing application configuration or JavaScript. It adds the module helper to layouts without script tags; customized script layouts are left unchanged with setup instructions. An explicit application turbo.js asset overrides the framework version. Ensure the layout contains:

<meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrf_token() }}">
{{ javascript_importmap_tags() }}

Load one Turbo runtime: replace an existing runtime rather than adding a second one. Run asset precompilation for production. Installation does not rewrite existing page views. To upgrade Turbo:

uv lock --upgrade-package flaskteroids-turbo
uv sync --locked
bin/flask assets:precompile

items.title: Frames and layouts
items.text:
A frame navigation replaces only the matching <turbo-frame> in the current page. Its destination must return a frame with the same ID.

New generated page templates use:

{% extends layout %}
{% block body %}
  <!-- Page content, including any frames. -->
{% endblock %}

layout selects layouts/application.html normally and layouts/turbo/frame.html for a request carrying Turbo-Frame. The minimal frame layout retains head and body blocks and the CSRF meta token. Override it in app/views/layouts/turbo/frame.html if needed. Set Controller.layout or frame_layout to another template path on a controller class, or assign self.layout / self.frame_layout in an action or callback before rendering.

Existing {% extends "layouts/application.html" %} templates still work: Turbo extracts the matching frame from the full page. Adopting {% extends layout %} is an optional rendering optimization, not a requirement for Frames.

Controllers expose self.turbo_frame_request (a boolean) and self.turbo_frame_request_id (the ID or None). Templates call turbo_frame_request() and turbo_frame_request_id() instead.

items.title: IDs and frame tags
items.text:
dom_id, dom_class, turbo_frame_tag, and turbo_stream are automatically available in Jinja. Python code can import them and the builder class:

from flaskteroids.turbo import (
    TurboStreamBuilder,
    dom_class,
    dom_id,
    turbo_frame_tag,
    turbo_stream,
)

For a Post with key 1, dom_id(post) is post_1, dom_id(post, "edit") is edit_post_1, and dom_class(post) is post. A record without a key, or the Post class, gives new_post; dom_id(Post, "edit") gives edit_post. Keys come from public Model.to_key(), not an overridden URL slug in to_param(). to_key() and to_partial_path() can be overridden for custom record identity and partial conventions.

{% call turbo_frame_tag(post) %}{{ post.title }}{% endcall %}
{% call turbo_frame_tag(post, "edit") %}...{% endcall %}
{% call turbo_frame_tag("post", "1", "comments") %}...{% endcall %}

{% call turbo_frame_tag("preview", src=post_path(post), loading="lazy", target="_top") %}
  Loading…
{% endcall %}

The compound ID above is post_1_comments. src also accepts a model destination, such as src=post or src=[post, comment]. A lazy frame fetches its source when visible; target="_top" makes navigation leave the frame.

Links and forms can target a frame, or opt out of Turbo:

{{ link_to("Edit", edit_post_path(post), data={"turbo_frame": dom_id(post)}) }}
{{ link_to("Full page", post_path(post), data={"turbo_frame": "_top"}) }}
{% call(form) form_with(model=post, data={"turbo": False}) %}
  {{ form.text_field("title") }}
  {{ form.submit("Save") }}
{% endcall %}

Frame/Stream tags, links, buttons, and form_with normalize class_ to class, nested data/aria keys to dashed attributes, and HTML boolean attributes such as disabled=True appropriately. data={"turbo": False} emits data-turbo="false", not an omitted attribute. Ordinary text and all attribute values are escaped. Use Markup only for trusted HTML; never apply |safe to user input.

items.title: Minimal inline edit
items.text:
Assume route.resources("posts") and a Post model with a title attribute. Use a record partial that is itself the frame, so rendering it in a list or a show page does not create duplicate DOM IDs:

<!-- app/views/posts/_post.html -->
{% call turbo_frame_tag(post) %}
  <p>{{ post.title }}</p>
  {{ link_to("Edit", edit_post_path(post)) }}
{% endcall %}

<!-- app/views/posts/show.html -->
{% extends layout %}
{% block body %}{{ render(post) }}{% endblock %}

<!-- app/views/posts/_form.html -->
{% for message in post.errors.full_messages() %}
  <p>{{ message }}</p>
{% endfor %}
{% call(form) form_with(model=post) %}
  {{ form.label("title") }}
  {{ form.text_field("title") }}
  {{ form.submit("Save") }}
{% endcall %}

<!-- app/views/posts/edit.html -->
{% extends layout %}
{% block body %}
  {% call turbo_frame_tag(post) %}
    {{ render(partial="posts/form", locals={"post": post}) }}
    {{ link_to("Cancel", post_path(post)) }}
  {% endcall %}
{% endblock %}

# app/controllers/posts_controller.py
from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.post import Post
from flaskteroids.routes import post_path


class PostsController(ApplicationController):
    def show(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])

    def edit(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])

    def update(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])
        if self.post.update(**self.params.expect(post=["title"])):
            return self.redirect_to(post_path(self.post), status=303)
        return self.render("edit", status=422)

Show, edit, validation redisplay, and the redirected show all contain the same post_1 frame. Return 422 for invalid HTML and use 303 See Other after a successful mutation. Ordinary Turbo POST forms support HTML fallback; a Stream response is not required. Generated scaffolds remain full-page CRUD by default, not inline-edit interfaces. New scaffold record IDs use dom_id underscores, and generated update redirects use 303.

items.title: HTTP Stream responses
items.text:
Streams can change several elements in one response, without a frame wrapper. Turbo forms advertise text/vnd.turbo-stream.html for unsafe submissions. GET links/forms opt in with data={"turbo_stream": True}:

{{ link_to("Load more", posts_path(page=2), data={"turbo_stream": True}) }}

items.title: Create: append a post and update a notice
items.text:
Add an index with a target container and the create form:

<!-- app/views/posts/index.html -->
{% extends layout %}
{% block body %}
  <div id="notice"></div>
  <div id="posts">
    {% for post in posts %}{{ render(post) }}{% endfor %}
  </div>
  {{ render(partial="posts/form", locals={"post": post}) }}
{% endblock %}

Add these actions to PostsController (the preceding imports still apply):

def index(self):
    self.posts = Post.all()
    self.post = Post.new()

def create(self):
    self.post = Post.new(**self.params.expect(post=["title"]))
    if self.post.save():
        return self.respond_to(
            html=lambda: self.redirect_to(post_path(self.post), status=303),
            turbo_stream=lambda: self.render(),
        )
    return self.render("new", status=422)

The HTML validation fallback needs app/views/posts/new.html:

{% extends layout %}
{% block body %}
  {{ render(partial="posts/form", locals={"post": post}) }}
{% endblock %}

The successful Stream response uses the conventional template, without page layout inheritance:

<!-- app/views/posts/create.turbo_stream.html -->
{{ turbo_stream.append("posts", post) }}
{{ turbo_stream.update("notice", "Post created") }}

post renders through posts/_post.html, which supplies its own frame ID. The non-Turbo HTML request redirects normally. A normal Turbo form can redisplay new.html with 422 when no new.turbo_stream.html exists and HTML is acceptable.

items.title: Builder and partials
items.text:
Use replace to redraw a record, update to change an element's contents, or remove to delete an element:

{{ turbo_stream.replace(post) }}
{{ turbo_stream.update("notice", partial="shared/notice", locals={"message": "Saved"}) }}
{{ turbo_stream.remove(post) }}

A record target supplies its conventional DOM ID and partial. In the first example, post renders through posts/_post.html. Ordinary string content is escaped; rendered partials supply HTML.

You can also build a response directly in an action:

return self.render(turbo_stream=[
    self.turbo_stream.remove(self.post),
    self.turbo_stream.update("notice", "Post removed"),
])

For reusable template fragments, see Render a partial.

items.title: Negotiation and routes
items.text:
self.respond_to(html=..., json=..., turbo_stream=...) selects an offered format. An implicit render selects <action>.turbo_stream.html when Streams are requested; it falls back to <action>.html if the Stream template is absent and HTML is acceptable. Stream responses use MIME type text/vnd.turbo-stream.html.

Accept quality values are honored. Equal-quality requests explicitly listing Streams use client format order; wildcard-only requests default to HTML. A request with no acceptable offered format returns 406. Resource helpers accept posts_path(format="turbo_stream") or post_path(post, format="turbo_stream") to force Streams via a .turbo_stream suffix; forced URLs require a Stream response rather than HTML fallback. Custom named routes do not automatically gain suffix support. See Routing.

Relative translations in posts/create.turbo_stream.html, such as t(".notice"), use posts.create.notice: the format suffix is not part of the translation scope.

items.title: Caching and security
items.text:
Controller HTML, JSON, and Stream responses vary on Accept and Turbo-Frame. For the application's framework response class, validators set with set_etag or add_etag track the original value and are partitioned by final MIME type and frame/page before make_conditional and final emission. Validators set on pending self.response transfer into the prepared response with that original value, so changing from HTML to JSON or Streams does not reuse an HTML validator.

This does not create validators or perform conditional handling automatically: set a validator and call response.make_conditional(request) yourself when needed. Manually constructed native Flask/Werkzeug Response objects and manually assigned ETag header strings remain application-owned and are not rewritten; provide representation-specific validators for those responses yourself.

These cache boundaries are not authorization or a shared-cache policy. A Turbo-Frame header is not proof of permission. Keep normal authentication, authorization, strong parameters and CSRF protection, and do not put session-specific pages or CSRF tokens in a shared cache.
